author: David McCullough
description: McCullough follows the American Revolution through a single pivotal year, tracing George Washington's untested army from the siege of Boston through defeats in New York to the surprise victory at Trenton. British commanders and ordinary soldiers on both sides receive close attention alongside the generals. Readers who enjoy narrative history built on letters and diaries will find a vivid, well-paced account of how near the cause came to collapse.

author: George Orwell
description: Winston Smith works at the Ministry of Truth in Oceania, a totalitarian state where the Party rewrites history, monitors citizens constantly and polices even private thought. His quiet rebellion, including a forbidden love affair, sets him against a regime that demands total loyalty. Orwell's dystopian novel remains a key reference point for discussions of surveillance, propaganda and the manipulation of language and truth.

title: 21 Lessons for the 21st Century
author: Yuval Noah Harari
description: Harari turns from the distant past to the present, examining the pressing questions facing humanity now. Chapters cover artificial intelligence and automation, the erosion of liberal democracy, nationalism, religion, terrorism, fake news and how to educate children for an uncertain future. Written as a series of short essays, it suits general readers who want a broad, provocative framework for thinking about current global challenges.

title: 802.11 Wireless Networks: The Definitive Guide
author: Matthew S. Gast
description: A technical guide to Wi-Fi networks based on the IEEE 802.11 standards. It explains the physical and MAC layers, security, deployment and analysis of wireless networks. Useful for engineers and administrators.

title: A Beautiful Mind
author: Sylvia Nasar
description: The biography of John Nash, the mathematician whose work in game theory earned a Nobel Prize in economics. Nasar describes his early brilliance, his long struggle with schizophrenia and his recovery. A portrait of genius and mental illness.

title: A Brief History of Time
author: Stephen Hawking
description: Hawking's popular account of cosmology traces how human understanding of the universe developed, from early models of the heavens through Newton and Einstein to modern ideas about the Big Bang and black holes. Along the way it explains how scientific thinking about space and time changed over centuries. Readers interested in the history of ideas will find an accessible overview written with almost no mathematics.

title: A People's History of the United States
author: Howard Zinn
description: Zinn retells American history from the viewpoint of groups often left out of standard textbooks, including Indigenous peoples, enslaved Africans, women, workers and immigrants. The narrative runs from Columbus to the modern era, emphasising protest movements, labour struggles and resistance to power. It offers a deliberately critical counterpoint to traditional accounts and suits readers who want to examine history from the bottom up.

title: A Promised Land
author: Barack Obama
description: The first volume of Barack Obama's presidential memoirs, covering his early political career, the 2008 election and much of his first term. He discusses major decisions on the economy, healthcare and foreign policy. Of interest to readers of politics and recent history.

title: A Random Walk Down Wall Street
author: Burton G. Malkiel
description: Malkiel makes the case that stock prices are hard to predict and that most investors are better served by low-cost, broadly diversified index funds than by trying to beat the market. He reviews technical and fundamental analysis, market bubbles, behavioural finance and asset allocation across life stages. Individual investors looking for a reasoned, long-term approach to building wealth will find practical guidance here.

title: A Room of One's Own
author: Virginia Woolf
description: Based on lectures Virginia Woolf gave at women's colleges in 1928, this essay argues that women need financial independence and private space to write. It examines the history of women and fiction. A foundational text in feminist literary criticism.

title: A Short History of Nearly Everything
author: Bill Bryson
description: Bryson sets out to understand how scientists know what they know, covering the origins of the universe, the age of the Earth, atoms, evolution, geology and the emergence of human beings. Much of the appeal lies in the stories of the often eccentric researchers behind major discoveries. Written with humour and curiosity, it works well for general readers wanting a wide-ranging introduction to science.

title: AI Superpowers
author: Kai-Fu Lee
publisher: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt Trade & Reference Publishers
description: Kai-Fu Lee compares the development of artificial intelligence in China and the United States and discusses its likely effects on jobs and society. He also reflects on the human qualities that machines cannot replace. A perspective on the global AI landscape.

title: Accelerate
author: Nicole Forsgren
description: Drawing on several years of survey research into software delivery, Forsgren, Humble and Kim identify the practices that distinguish high-performing technology organisations. The book explains measures such as deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore service, and links them to capabilities in architecture, culture and continuous delivery. Engineering leaders and DevOps practitioners will find evidence-based guidance for improving delivery performance.

title: Alan Turing: The Enigma
author: Andrew Hodges
description: The definitive biography of Alan Turing, the mathematician who laid foundations for computer science and helped break German codes during the Second World War. Hodges covers his work, his persecution for homosexuality and his death. Important reading for computer science and history students.

title: Alexander Hamilton
author: Ron Chernow
description: Chernow traces the life of Alexander Hamilton from his difficult childhood in the Caribbean to his role as Washington's aide, co-author of the Federalist Papers and first Secretary of the Treasury. The biography examines his financial system, political rivalries with Jefferson and Adams, personal scandals and fatal duel with Aaron Burr. Readers interested in the founding of the United States will find a detailed, richly documented portrait.

title: Algorithm Design
author: Jon Kleinberg
description: A textbook that teaches how to design algorithms by working from real problems to solutions. It covers greedy methods, divide and conquer, dynamic programming, network flow, NP-completeness, approximation and randomised algorithms. Aimed at upper-level undergraduate and graduate algorithms courses.

title: Algorithms
author: Robert Sedgewick
description: Sedgewick and Wayne present the essential algorithms and data structures every programmer should know, including sorting, searching, symbol tables, graphs and string processing. Implementations are given in Java, with an emphasis on performance analysis and scientific study of running times. Undergraduate students and self-taught developers will find a practical, well-illustrated textbook that connects theory to real code.

title: Algorithms to Live By
author: Brian Christian
description: The authors show how ideas from computer science, such as optimal stopping, sorting, caching, scheduling and game theory, can inform everyday decisions. Each chapter explains an algorithmic idea in plain language and applies it to human situations. An accessible read for general audiences and students.

title: An Introduction to Database Systems
author: C. J. Date
description: C. J. Date's long-standing textbook on database theory and practice, with a strong focus on the relational model. It covers relational algebra and calculus, normalisation, integrity, views, recovery and concurrency. A classic reference for database students.

title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning
author: Gareth James
description: An accessible introduction to statistical learning methods such as regression, classification, resampling, regularisation, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering. Each chapter includes labs in R or Python. Suited to undergraduates and practitioners.

title: Animal Farm
author: George Orwell
description: Orwell's short allegorical fable tells of farm animals who overthrow their human owner hoping to create a society of equals. Over time the pigs take control, and the revolution's ideals are gradually twisted into a new form of tyranny. Read as a satire of the Russian Revolution and Stalinism, it suits readers of all ages interested in power, propaganda and political corruption.

title: Applied Cryptography
author: Bruce Schneier
description: Bruce Schneier's comprehensive reference to cryptographic protocols, algorithms and source code. It covers symmetric and public-key cryptography, digital signatures, key management and practical protocol design. A classic for security engineers.

title: Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans
author: Melanie Mitchell
description: Melanie Mitchell explains how current AI systems work, including deep learning for vision, games and language, and where they still fall short. She separates real progress from hype. Clear reading for students and general audiences.

title: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach
author: Stuart Russell
description: Russell and Norvig provide a comprehensive textbook on artificial intelligence built around the idea of rational agents. Topics include search, logic, planning, probabilistic reasoning, machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, robotics and the ethics of AI. Widely used in university courses, it suits students and practitioners who want a rigorous, broad grounding in both classical and modern approaches to the field.

title: Astrophysics for People in a Hurry
author: Neil deGrasse Tyson
description: Tyson offers a compact tour of the universe in a series of short chapters on the Big Bang, gravity, light, dark matter, dark energy, galaxies and the search for exoplanets. Each topic is explained in plain language with occasional humour. Busy readers who want a quick, accessible overview of what modern astrophysics has discovered will find it easy to read in short sittings.

title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear
description: Clear argues that small, consistent improvements compound over time into significant results. He presents a practical framework for building good habits and breaking bad ones by making cues obvious, cravings attractive, responses easy and rewards satisfying, and stresses the role of identity in lasting change. Readers seeking concrete, actionable techniques for personal growth, productivity or health will find clear examples throughout.

title: Attached
author: Amir Levine
description: A psychiatrist and a psychologist explain adult attachment theory and the three main attachment styles: anxious, avoidant and secure. They show how these styles affect romantic relationships. Practical reading for anyone interested in relationships.

title: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python
author: Al Sweigart
description: A beginner-friendly introduction to Python focused on practical scripts for everyday tasks. Readers learn the basics of the language, then use it to work with files, spreadsheets, PDFs, web pages, email and the keyboard and mouse. No prior programming experience is assumed.

title: Awaken the Giant Within
author: Tony Robbins
description: Robbins presents strategies for taking control of emotions, finances, relationships and physical health. Central themes include the power of decisions, changing limiting beliefs, the questions people habitually ask themselves and conditioning new emotional patterns. Structured with exercises and practical steps, it suits readers looking for a structured self-improvement programme focused on goal setting and personal change.

title: BGP
author: Iljitsch van Beijnum
description: An introduction to the Border Gateway Protocol, which routes traffic between networks on the internet. The book covers BGP operation, configuration, routing policy, multihoming and traffic engineering. Practical for network administrators.

title: Bad Blood
author: John Carreyrou
description: A Wall Street Journal reporter recounts the rise and fall of Theranos, a start-up that claimed to run many blood tests from a finger prick. Carreyrou describes the company's culture, the investors and the whistleblowers who helped expose it. A cautionary tale about technology, ethics and corporate governance.

title: Band of Brothers
author: Stephen E. Ambrose
description: Ambrose follows Easy Company of the US Army's 101st Airborne Division from training in 1942 through the Normandy landings and the end of the war in Europe. Based on interviews with veterans, it focuses on the soldiers' experiences. A well-known account of the Second World War.

title: Becoming
author: Michelle Obama
description: Michelle Obama recounts her life from a working-class childhood on Chicago's South Side through Princeton, Harvard Law School and a career in law and public service. She describes balancing family with her husband's political rise and her eight years as First Lady. The memoir offers a personal perspective on identity, ambition, motherhood and public life, appealing to readers of biography and contemporary American history.

title: Behave
author: Robert M. Sapolsky
description: A neuroscientist and primatologist explains human behaviour by working backwards in time, from the brain activity a second before an action to hormones, childhood, culture and evolution. Sapolsky covers violence, cooperation and morality. A wide-ranging, detailed book.

title: Benjamin Franklin: An American Life
author: Walter Isaacson
description: Walter Isaacson's biography of Benjamin Franklin, covering his work as a printer, writer, scientist, inventor, diplomat and founding father of the United States. The book places his achievements in historical context. A readable biography for general readers and history students.

title: Between the World and Me
author: Ta-Nehisi Coates
description: Written as a letter to his teenage son, this book reflects on what it means to be Black in the United States. Coates draws on his own childhood, education and history to discuss race, violence and vulnerability. A short, personal work of social commentary.

title: Big Magic
author: Elizabeth Gilbert
description: Elizabeth Gilbert shares her views on creativity, fear and inspiration, encouraging readers to pursue creative work for its own sake. The book mixes personal stories with practical encouragement. Aimed at anyone wanting to live a more creative life.

title: Black Hat Python
author: Justin Seitz
description: Justin Seitz shows how to write Python tools for security testing, including network sniffers, web scanners, trojans and forensic scripts. It is aimed at penetration testers and security researchers. Some programming background is assumed.

title: Blink
author: Malcolm Gladwell
description: Gladwell explores rapid cognition, the snap judgements people make in the first moments of encountering something. Using examples from art authentication, speed dating, military exercises and emergency medicine, he examines when quick intuitive decisions outperform careful analysis and when they lead to bias and error. General readers interested in psychology and decision-making will find an engaging, story-driven introduction to the topic.

title: Blockchain Basics
author: Daniel Drescher
description: Drescher explains how blockchain technology works without requiring a background in mathematics or programming. Concepts such as hashing, cryptographic signatures, distributed ledgers, consensus and mining are introduced step by step in short, focused chapters. Managers, students and curious readers who want to understand the underlying ideas behind cryptocurrencies and distributed ledgers will find a clear, non-technical starting point.

title: Blue Ocean Strategy
author: W. Chan Kim
description: Kim and Mauborgne argue that companies grow most successfully not by fighting rivals in crowded markets but by creating uncontested market space where competition becomes irrelevant. They offer analytical tools such as the strategy canvas and the four actions framework, illustrated with case studies across many industries. Business leaders, entrepreneurs and strategy students will find a structured method for pursuing innovation in value.

title: Born a Crime
author: Trevor Noah
description: Trevor Noah's memoir of growing up in South Africa during and after apartheid, as the child of a Black mother and a white father at a time when such relationships were illegal. The book combines humour with serious reflection on race, poverty and family. Popular with both young adults and adults.

title: Boundaries
author: Henry Cloud
description: Two clinical psychologists explain how to set healthy limits in relationships with family, friends, partners and colleagues. They describe common boundary problems and offer guidance on saying no and taking responsibility for one's own choices. Written from a Christian perspective.

title: Brave New World
author: Aldous Huxley
description: Huxley imagines a future World State where people are engineered in laboratories, conditioned into fixed social castes and kept content through consumerism, casual sex and a drug called soma. Stability is achieved at the cost of art, family, individuality and deep feeling. When an outsider raised on a reservation enters this society, the novel questions what is lost in the pursuit of comfort and control.

title: Brief Answers to the Big Questions
author: Stephen Hawking
description: Stephen Hawking's final book addresses questions such as how the universe began, whether there is other intelligent life, and whether we can predict the future. Short chapters present his views in accessible language. A good introduction to his thinking.

title: Building Microservices
author: Sam Newman
description: Sam Newman explains how to design, build and run systems made of small, independently deployable services. Topics include modelling services, integration, testing, deployment, monitoring, security and organisational impact. A standard reference for software architects.

title: Built to Last
author: Jim Collins
description: A study of companies that remained leaders in their industries over many decades, compared with similar firms that fell behind. The authors identify shared traits such as a core ideology, bold goals and a culture that preserves values while encouraging progress. Aimed at managers and business students.

title: Built to Sell
author: John Warrillow
description: Through a story about an agency owner, Warrillow explains how to create a business that can run without its founder and be sold. Key ideas include standardising a product, reducing dependence on the owner and creating predictable revenue. Practical for small business owners.

title: CCNA Routing and Switching
author: Wendell Odom
description: Odom's certification guide prepares candidates for the Cisco CCNA Routing and Switching exams. It covers Ethernet LANs, switching, VLANs, IPv4 and IPv6 addressing and subnetting, routing protocols, access control lists and network troubleshooting. Practice questions, review exercises and configuration examples support structured study, making it suitable for networking students and IT professionals pursuing Cisco certification.

title: Can't Hurt Me
author: David Goggins
description: Goggins describes his journey from a childhood marked by poverty, abuse and racism to becoming a Navy SEAL and endurance athlete. He argues that most people use only a fraction of their capacity and sets out mental strategies for pushing past discomfort and self-imposed limits. Each chapter ends with a personal challenge, aimed at readers seeking motivation built on discipline and resilience.

title: Chip War
author: Chris Miller
description: A history of the semiconductor industry from its origins in the United States to today's global supply chain. Miller explains how control of chip design and manufacturing became central to economic and military power. Relevant to readers interested in technology, geopolitics and business.

title: Churchill: Walking with Destiny
author: Andrew Roberts
description: Andrew Roberts draws on newly available sources to write a single-volume life of Winston Churchill, from his youth through his wartime leadership to old age. He examines both his successes and his mistakes. A comprehensive biography of a major twentieth-century figure.

title: Clean Agile
author: Robert C. Martin
description: Martin revisits the original intentions behind agile software development, drawing on his involvement with its early days. He explains core practices such as short iterations, test-driven development, refactoring, pair programming and simple design, and explains how business and technical roles should work together. Developers and managers who want to understand agile principles beyond certifications and frameworks will find a direct, opinionated guide.

title: Clean Architecture
author: Robert C. Martin
description: Good architecture, in Martin's view, allows key decisions about frameworks, databases and delivery mechanisms to be deferred while protecting core business rules. The book works from programming paradigms and SOLID design up to components, layers and boundaries, with case studies showing how the ideas apply. It suits experienced programmers moving into design and architecture responsibilities.

title: Clean Code
author: Robert C. Martin
description: Martin presents practices for writing code that is easy to read, understand and change. Chapters address meaningful naming, small focused functions, comments, formatting, error handling, unit testing and class design, followed by case studies that refactor messy code step by step. Programmers at any stage who want to improve the quality and craftsmanship of their everyday code will find concrete, example-driven advice.

title: Click Here to Kill Everybody
author: Bruce Schneier
description: Schneier discusses the security risks of the internet of things, where connected devices control physical systems. He explains why insecurity persists and argues for government regulation and better design. Thought-provoking reading on technology policy.

title: Code Complete
author: Steve McConnell
description: McConnell gathers research and practical experience on the construction phase of software development into a single comprehensive handbook. It covers design in construction, variable naming, routines, control structures, defensive programming, debugging, refactoring, code tuning and collaborative practices such as reviews. Developers of all levels will find a language-independent reference for writing better code, supported by checklists and many examples.

title: Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software
author: Charles Petzold
description: Petzold builds up an explanation of how computers work, starting from simple codes like Morse and Braille and moving through relays, logic gates, binary arithmetic, memory and processors. It requires no technical background. A good companion for students beginning computer science or electronics.

title: CompTIA Network+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide
author: Mike Meyers
description: A study guide for the CompTIA Network+ certification, covering network models, cabling, TCP/IP, routing, switching, wireless, security and troubleshooting. Includes practice questions. Suitable for exam candidates and networking beginners.

title: Competitive Strategy
author: Michael E. Porter
description: Porter's classic framework for analysing industries and competitors, including the five forces that shape competition and the generic strategies firms can adopt. It provides tools for understanding industry structure and positioning. A core text in business strategy courses.

title: Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools
author: Alfred V. Aho
description: Commonly known as the Dragon Book, Aho and colleagues' text is a standard reference on compiler design. It covers lexical analysis, parsing, syntax-directed translation, type checking, intermediate code generation, runtime environments, code generation and optimisation. Computer science students and engineers working on programming languages or tools will find a thorough treatment of both theory and implementation techniques.

title: Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach
author: Sanjeev Arora
description: A graduate-level textbook on computational complexity theory, covering P and NP, space complexity, the polynomial hierarchy, randomised computation, interactive proofs, circuit lower bounds and PCP theorems. It combines classical results with more recent developments. Intended for advanced students and researchers in theoretical computer science.

title: Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach
author: John L. Hennessy
description: Hennessy and Patterson analyse computer design using quantitative measures of performance, cost and power. Topics include instruction-level parallelism, memory hierarchy, data-level and thread-level parallelism, warehouse-scale computers and domain-specific architectures. Aimed at graduate students and practising engineers, it offers an in-depth, data-driven view of how modern processors and systems are designed and evaluated.

title: Computer Networking
author: Andrew S. Tanenbaum
description: Tanenbaum's networking text works through the layers of a computer network from the physical medium up to applications. It explains data link protocols, medium access, routing, congestion control, transport protocols such as TCP and UDP, and application services, with attention to wireless networks and security. Students and professionals wanting a thorough, systematic grounding in how networks operate will find clear explanations and many real-world examples.

title: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach
author: James F. Kurose
description: Kurose and Ross introduce computer networking by starting at the application layer and working down through transport, network, link and physical layers. Familiar examples such as the web, email and DNS lead into deeper topics including TCP congestion control, routing algorithms, wireless and mobile networks and network security. Undergraduates and self-learners will find an approachable textbook with exercises and hands-on labs.

title: Computer Networks and Internets
author: Douglas E. Comer
description: Douglas Comer's introductory textbook on networking, covering data communications, packet switching, local and wide area networks, internetworking and network applications. Written for students taking a first networking course.

title: Computer Organization and Design
author: David A. Patterson
description: Patterson and Hennessy explain how computers work at the boundary between hardware and software. The book covers instruction sets, computer arithmetic, processor datapath and control, pipelining, memory hierarchy and parallel processors, using a real instruction set architecture throughout. It is well suited to undergraduate students in computer science and engineering who are taking a first course in computer architecture.

title: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
author: Randal E. Bryant
description: Bryant and O'Hallaron describe computer systems from the viewpoint of a programmer rather than a hardware designer. Topics include data representation, machine-level code, processor architecture, program optimisation, memory hierarchy, linking, exceptional control flow, virtual memory, system-level I/O, network programming and concurrency. Students and developers who want to write faster, more reliable programs by understanding what happens beneath their code will find it valuable.

title: Concrete Mathematics
author: Ronald L. Graham
description: A mathematics textbook covering the techniques most useful for analysing algorithms, including sums, recurrences, integer functions, binomial coefficients, generating functions and asymptotics. It grew out of a Stanford course and includes many exercises with answers. Suited to computer science students with a solid maths foundation.

title: Continuous Delivery
author: Jez Humble
description: Humble and Farley explain how to make software releases reliable, repeatable and low-risk through automation. The book introduces the deployment pipeline and covers version control, automated testing, continuous integration, configuration management, infrastructure and database changes. Developers, testers and operations staff looking to shorten the path from code commit to production will find a detailed and practical guide.

title: Cosmos
author: Carl Sagan
description: Sagan takes readers on a journey through space and time, exploring the evolution of the universe, the formation of stars and planets, the origins of life and the history of scientific discovery. He links astronomy to human culture, philosophy and the future of civilisation. Written with warmth and wonder, it suits general readers who want a thoughtful introduction to our place in the cosmos.

title: Countdown to Zero Day
author: Kim Zetter
description: Kim Zetter investigates Stuxnet, the computer worm designed to sabotage Iran's nuclear programme. The book explains how security researchers discovered and analysed it, and what it meant for cyber warfare. A detailed work of technology journalism.

title: Cracking the Coding Interview
author: Gayle Laakmann McDowell
description: McDowell, a former software engineering interviewer, prepares candidates for technical interviews at technology companies. The book reviews core data structures, algorithms and problem-solving strategies, and includes many programming questions with detailed solutions. Advice on behavioural questions, resumes and the hiring process is also included, making it useful for students and developers preparing for coding interviews.

title: Crossing the Chasm
author: Geoffrey A. Moore
description: Moore explains why many technology products struggle to move from early adopters to mainstream customers. He describes the technology adoption life cycle and offers a strategy for targeting a niche market to cross the gap. A standard read for marketers and technology entrepreneurs.

title: Cryptography Engineering
author: Niels Ferguson
description: A practical guide to designing and implementing cryptographic systems correctly. The authors cover block ciphers, hash functions, message authentication, key negotiation, randomness and public-key infrastructure. Useful for developers building secure software.

title: DNS and BIND
author: Paul Albitz
description: Albitz and Liu explain the Domain Name System and how to run it using BIND, the widely used name server software. Topics include zone files, name server configuration, delegation, security, troubleshooting, dynamic updates and DNSSEC. System and network administrators responsible for maintaining DNS infrastructure will find a detailed reference combining conceptual explanation with practical configuration examples.

title: Daring Greatly
author: Brené Brown
description: Brown draws on her research into shame and vulnerability to argue that willingness to be seen, take risks and face uncertainty is a source of courage, connection and creativity rather than weakness. She examines how shame shapes behaviour in families, schools and workplaces and suggests ways to build resilience against it. Readers interested in emotional wellbeing, parenting or leadership will find research-based insight.

title: Data Communications and Networking
author: Behrouz A. Forouzan
description: Forouzan's textbook introduces data communications and networking using a layered approach, from the physical layer to the application layer. It includes many figures, examples and exercises. Popular in undergraduate courses, especially in India.

title: Data Science from Scratch
author: Joel Grus
description: Joel Grus teaches data science fundamentals by implementing tools in plain Python, including statistics, gradient descent, regression, clustering, neural networks and recommender systems. Good for learners who want to understand methods from the ground up.

title: Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis in C++
author: Mark Allen Weiss
description: A textbook that teaches core data structures, such as lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables, heaps and graphs, alongside the analysis of algorithms that use them. Examples are written in C++, and the book covers sorting and algorithm design techniques. Designed for second-year data structures courses.

title: Data and Goliath
author: Bruce Schneier
description: Schneier examines mass surveillance by governments and companies, explaining how data is collected and used and why it matters for privacy and freedom. He proposes legal and technical responses. Relevant to students of security, law and policy.

title: Database Design for Mere Mortals
author: Michael J. Hernandez
description: Hernandez offers a practical introduction to relational database design that does not depend on any particular database product. He walks through gathering requirements, defining tables and fields, keys, relationships, business rules and views, with emphasis on sound structure and data integrity. Beginners, developers and business users who need to design reliable databases without heavy theory will find it approachable.

title: Database Internals
author: Alex Petrov
description: Alex Petrov explains how database storage engines and distributed databases work under the hood. Topics include B-trees, log-structured storage, transaction processing, replication and consensus algorithms. Useful for engineers who build or operate data systems.

title: Database Management Systems
author: Raghu Ramakrishnan
description: A textbook on the design and implementation of database systems, covering relational algebra, SQL, storage, indexing, query evaluation and optimisation, transactions and database design. It balances theory with system internals. Used in undergraduate and graduate courses.

title: Database Reliability Engineering
author: Laine Campbell
description: Campbell and Majors apply site reliability engineering ideas to databases, covering service levels, risk management, infrastructure, backup and recovery, security and operational practices. Useful for engineers responsible for production databases.

title: Database System Concepts
author: Abraham Silberschatz
description: Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan provide a comprehensive textbook on database systems. It covers the relational model, SQL, entity-relationship design, normalisation, storage and indexing, query processing and optimisation, transactions, concurrency control, recovery and distributed databases. Widely used in university courses, it suits students and professionals who want a solid grounding in both database theory and the internals of database management systems.

title: Deep Learning
author: Ian Goodfellow
description: Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville present a rigorous treatment of deep learning, beginning with the necessary linear algebra, probability and numerical computation. The core chapters cover feedforward networks, regularisation, optimisation, convolutional and recurrent networks, followed by research topics such as autoencoders and generative models. Graduate students and researchers seeking the mathematical foundations of modern neural networks will find a thorough reference.

title: Deep Learning for Coders with fastai and PyTorch
author: Jeremy Howard
description: A hands-on introduction to deep learning for programmers, using the fastai library and PyTorch to build models for images, text, tabular data and recommendations. It explains the theory progressively through code. Suitable for developers without advanced mathematics.

title: Deep Learning with Python
author: François Chollet
description: Chollet, the creator of Keras, introduces deep learning through hands-on Python code. Readers move from the basics of neural networks to computer vision, text and sequence processing, and generative models, with intuitive explanations in place of heavy mathematics. Programmers with some Python experience who want to build practical deep learning applications will find clear examples and sensible advice on model development.

title: Deep Work
author: Cal Newport
description: Newport argues that the ability to concentrate without distraction on cognitively demanding tasks is increasingly rare and increasingly valuable. He explains why focused work matters and offers strategies for building it, such as scheduling deep work, embracing boredom, limiting social media and reducing shallow tasks. Knowledge workers and students wanting to produce better work in less time will find practical rules to adopt.

title: Delivering Happiness
author: Tony Hsieh
description: Tony Hsieh describes his path from early ventures to leading the online retailer Zappos, focusing on customer service and company culture. He explains how the company built its values. A business memoir for readers interested in culture-driven companies.

title: Design Patterns
author: Erich Gamma
description: Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides catalogue twenty-three reusable solutions to recurring problems in object-oriented software design. Patterns are grouped as creational, structural and behavioural, and each is described with its intent, structure, participants, consequences and sample code. Developers and software architects seeking a shared vocabulary for designing flexible, maintainable object-oriented systems will find it a foundational reference.

title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
author: Martin Kleppmann
description: Kleppmann examines the principles behind the systems used to store and process data at scale. Topics include data models, storage engines, encoding, replication, partitioning, transactions, consistency and consensus, along with batch and stream processing. Software engineers and architects who need to understand the trade-offs among databases and distributed data tools will find a clear, carefully reasoned guide grounded in real systems.

title: Die with Zero
author: Bill Perkins
description: Perkins argues that people often save too much for too long and miss experiences that matter most at particular ages. He offers ways to plan spending, giving and work so that money supports a fulfilling life. A thought-provoking read on personal finance and life planning.

title: Digital Design and Computer Architecture
author: David Money Harris
description: A textbook that moves from digital logic and hardware description languages to the design of a working processor. It covers combinational and sequential circuits, assembly language, microarchitecture and memory systems. Aimed at students in introductory computer architecture and digital design courses.

title: Discipline Equals Freedom
author: Jocko Willink
description: A short field manual by former Navy SEAL officer Jocko Willink on building self-discipline. It covers mindset, sleep, nutrition and physical training, with workout plans. Direct and practical for readers seeking structure.

title: Disciplined Entrepreneurship
author: Bill Aulet
description: A step-by-step framework from MIT for building a new venture, covering market segmentation, customer profiling, value proposition, business model and product planning. Each step includes worked examples. Suited to students and first-time founders.

title: Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications
author: Kenneth H. Rosen
description: A comprehensive introduction to discrete mathematics for computing, covering logic, proofs, sets, functions, counting, probability, relations, graphs, trees and Boolean algebra. Each topic is linked to applications in computer science, with extensive exercises. A standard text for first-year discrete maths courses.

title: Distributed Systems
author: Maarten van Steen
description: Van Steen and Tanenbaum explain the principles and paradigms of distributed systems, where independent computers cooperate to appear as a single coherent system. Chapters cover architectures, processes, communication, naming, coordination, consistency and replication, fault tolerance and security. Students and engineers seeking a structured introduction to how distributed systems are designed and why they behave as they do will find balanced coverage of theory and practice.

title: Don't Make Me Think
author: Steve Krug
description: Steve Krug's guide to web and mobile usability, explaining how people actually use websites and how to design clear, simple interfaces. It includes advice on navigation, page layout and running inexpensive usability tests. Short and practical for designers and developers.

title: Dreams from My Father
author: Barack Obama
description: Barack Obama's memoir, written before his political career, about his childhood in Hawaii and Indonesia, his search for identity and his visit to his father's family in Kenya. It reflects on race, family and belonging. A personal account of identity and heritage.

title: Drive
author: Daniel H. Pink
description: Daniel Pink argues that people are motivated more by autonomy, mastery and purpose than by rewards and punishments for many kinds of work. He draws on research in psychology and economics. Useful for students, teachers, managers and parents.

title: Dune
author: Frank Herbert
description: On the desert planet Arrakis, the only source of a valuable spice, young Paul Atreides and his family become entangled in a deadly struggle between noble houses. Forced into the deep desert, Paul joins the native Fremen and confronts questions of destiny and power. Herbert's science fiction novel blends politics, religion and ecology, and suits readers who enjoy richly built worlds.

title: Educated
author: Tara Westover
description: Westover recounts growing up in a survivalist family in rural Idaho, where she did not attend school and was kept away from doctors. Through self-teaching she gained entry to university and eventually earned a doctorate from Cambridge. The memoir explores family loyalty, memory and the cost of education that changes who one is, and appeals to readers of personal narrative and resilience.

title: Effective C++
author: Scott Meyers
description: A collection of specific guidelines for writing better C++, each explained with examples and reasoning. Topics include resource management, constructors and destructors, inheritance, templates and designing clear interfaces. Intended for programmers who already know C++ basics.

title: Effective Java
author: Joshua Bloch
description: Bloch presents best practices for writing robust, efficient and maintainable Java, organised as a series of focused items. Guidance covers object creation, classes and interfaces, generics, enums, lambdas and streams, methods, exceptions, concurrency and serialisation. Intermediate and experienced Java programmers who want to use the language and its libraries more effectively will find concise, well-reasoned advice.

title: Ego Is the Enemy
author: Ryan Holiday
publisher: Portfolio / Penguin, an imprint ofPenguin Random House LLC
description: Ryan Holiday draws on historical figures and Stoic philosophy to show how ego can block learning, success and recovery from failure. The book is divided into stages of aspiration, success and failure. A reflective read on humility and self-awareness.

title: Einstein: His Life and Universe
author: Walter Isaacson
description: Isaacson traces Albert Einstein's life from his youth in Germany through his remarkable work on relativity and quantum theory to his later years in the United States. The biography draws on Einstein's personal letters to portray his relationships, politics, religious views and nonconformist character. Readers interested in science and its history will find the physics explained accessibly alongside a full human portrait.

title: Elasticsearch: The Definitive Guide
author: Clinton Gormley
description: A guide to Elasticsearch, the open-source search and analytics engine. It covers indexing, searching, relevance scoring, aggregations and running clusters. Useful for developers adding search to applications.

title: Elon Musk
author: Ashlee Vance
description: Vance profiles Elon Musk, following his upbringing in South Africa, move to North America and early internet ventures through to the founding of SpaceX and his leadership of Tesla. Based on extensive interviews, it examines Musk's ambitions, demanding management style and the risks he took. Readers interested in entrepreneurship and the modern technology industry will find a detailed look at his career.

title: Eloquent JavaScript
author: Marijn Haverbeke
description: Haverbeke teaches programming through JavaScript, starting with values, functions and data structures and moving on to higher-order functions, objects, asynchronous programming and modules. Later chapters apply the language in the browser and with Node.js, including several project chapters. Beginners and those wanting a deeper understanding of JavaScript will find exercises that build genuine programming skill rather than just syntax.

title: Emotional Intelligence
author: Daniel Goleman
description: Goleman argues that abilities such as self-awareness, self-control, empathy and social skill can matter as much as conventional intelligence for success and wellbeing. Drawing on psychology and brain research, he explains how emotions shape thinking and how these capacities can be learned and strengthened. Parents, educators, managers and general readers interested in human behaviour will find the ideas widely applicable.

title: Engineering a Compiler
author: Keith D. Cooper
description: A textbook on building modern compilers, from scanning and parsing through intermediate representations, optimisation, instruction selection, register allocation and scheduling. It emphasises practical engineering trade-offs alongside the underlying theory. Suitable for undergraduate and graduate compiler courses.

title: Entangled Life
author: Merlin Sheldrake
description: A biologist explores the world of fungi, from networks that connect plant roots to yeasts, moulds and mushrooms. Sheldrake explains how fungi shape ecosystems, medicine and human culture. An engaging work of popular biology.

title: Essentialism
author: Greg McKeown
description: McKeown advocates a disciplined pursuit of less, focusing time and energy only on what is truly important. He explains how to distinguish the vital few from the trivial many, say no gracefully, eliminate non-essential commitments and build routines that make important work easier. Professionals feeling overcommitted or stretched thin will find a practical approach to prioritisation and decision-making.

title: Extreme Ownership
author: Jocko Willink
description: Two former US Navy SEAL officers apply lessons from combat leadership in Iraq to business. Each chapter pairs a battlefield account with a principle, such as taking ownership of outcomes, and a business example. Practical reading for team leaders and managers.

title: Factfulness
author: Hans Rosling
description: A physician and statistician explains why many people hold an overly negative view of global trends in health, wealth and education. Rosling identifies common thinking habits that distort understanding and shows how to check claims against data. Useful for students and anyone who works with statistics.

title: Fast Food Nation
author: Eric Schlosser
description: An investigation of the American fast food industry, from its origins in post-war California to its effects on agriculture, meatpacking, labour and public health. Schlosser combines reporting with economic and historical context. A widely discussed work of investigative journalism.

title: Feeling Good
author: David D. Burns
description: A psychiatrist presents cognitive behavioural techniques for overcoming depression, such as identifying and challenging distorted thoughts. The book includes exercises and self-assessment tools. A long-standing self-help guide grounded in clinical research.

title: Flash Boys
author: Michael Lewis
description: An account of high-frequency trading in US stock markets and a group of traders who set out to expose how speed advantages affected ordinary investors. Lewis explains market structure, exchanges and order routing in plain language. Of interest to readers curious about modern financial markets and technology.

title: Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience
author: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
description: Csikszentmihalyi describes flow, a state of deep absorption in which people feel fully engaged and lose track of time. Based on years of research, he explores the conditions that produce it, such as clear goals, immediate feedback and a balance between challenge and skill, and how it applies to work, leisure and relationships. Readers interested in happiness and positive psychology will find it insightful.

title: Fluent Python
author: Luciano Ramalho
description: An in-depth guide to writing idiomatic Python by understanding the language's data model, data structures, functions, objects and concurrency features. Each chapter explains why Python behaves as it does, with many runnable examples. Best for programmers who already know basic Python and want to master it.

title: Founders at Work
author: Jessica Livingston
description: Jessica Livingston interviews founders of well-known technology companies about their early days, including how they found ideas, raised money and survived setbacks. The interviews show how messy and uncertain starting a company can be. Valuable reading for aspiring entrepreneurs.

title: Four Thousand Weeks
author: Oliver Burkeman
description: Starting from the fact that an average lifetime is about four thousand weeks, Burkeman questions conventional productivity advice. He argues for accepting limits, choosing priorities deliberately and tolerating unfinished tasks. A thoughtful read for people who feel overwhelmed by busyness.

title: Freakonomics
author: Steven D. Levitt
description: Economist Levitt and journalist Dubner apply economic thinking and data analysis to unexpected questions, such as cheating among teachers and sumo wrestlers, the finances of drug gangs and the influence of parenting choices. The book shows how incentives shape behaviour and how conventional wisdom can be misleading. Curious readers who enjoy counterintuitive ideas will find it an entertaining introduction to economic reasoning.

title: Freedom at Midnight
author: Larry Collins
description: Collins and Lapierre recount the events surrounding Indian independence and partition in 1947, from the final months of British rule to the violence that followed. The book draws on interviews with many of the people involved. A vivid narrative history for general readers.

title: Fundamentals of Database Systems
author: Ramez Elmasri
description: A comprehensive textbook covering data modelling, the relational model, SQL, normalisation, storage and indexing, query processing, transactions, concurrency and recovery. It also introduces NoSQL and big data topics. Widely used in university database courses.

title: Games People Play
author: Eric Berne
description: Eric Berne describes the repeated patterns of interaction, or games, that people use in relationships, based on his theory of transactional analysis. He catalogues common games and their hidden motives. A classic of popular psychology.

title: Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World
author: Jack Weatherford
description: Weatherford reassesses Genghis Khan and the Mongol Empire, tracing his rise from a harsh childhood on the steppe to the conquest of vast territories. He argues that Mongol rule opened trade routes, spread technology and ideas, and encouraged religious tolerance in ways that shaped later Eurasian history. Readers interested in world history will find a lively narrative that challenges common stereotypes.

title: Getting Things Done
author: David Allen
description: David Allen's productivity method for capturing every task and commitment in a trusted external system, then deciding the next physical action for each. It explains how to organise projects, lists and weekly reviews so the mind is free to focus. Useful for students and professionals juggling many responsibilities.

title: Getting to Yes
author: Roger Fisher
description: From the Harvard Negotiation Project, this book outlines principled negotiation: separating people from the problem, focusing on interests, generating options and using objective criteria. It is short and practical. A standard introduction to negotiation for students and professionals.

title: Ghost in the Wires
author: Kevin Mitnick
description: Mitnick recounts his years as one of the most wanted computer hackers in the United States, describing how he broke into phone networks and corporate systems while evading the FBI. Much of his success relied on social engineering, manipulating people into revealing information. Readers interested in cybersecurity, hacking culture or true crime will find a first-person account with useful lessons about human vulnerabilities.

title: Good Strategy Bad Strategy
author: Richard P. Rumelt
description: Rumelt explains what makes a strategy effective: a clear diagnosis, a guiding policy and coherent actions. He contrasts this with common failures such as vague goals and fluff, using examples from business and history. Useful for managers, students and anyone responsible for planning.

title: Good to Great
author: Jim Collins
description: Collins and his research team compared companies that made a sustained leap from average to outstanding performance with similar firms that did not. Their findings include humble yet determined leadership, getting the right people in place, confronting hard facts, focusing on a core concept and building a culture of discipline. Managers and business readers interested in long-term organisational success will find research-based lessons.

title: Grant
author: Ron Chernow
description: Ron Chernow's biography of Ulysses S. Grant, covering his early struggles, his leadership of Union armies in the American Civil War and his presidency. It reassesses his record on Reconstruction and civil rights. A long, detailed biography for history readers.

title: Graph Databases
author: Ian Robinson
description: An introduction to graph databases, explaining how to model data as nodes and relationships and query it efficiently. Examples use Neo4j and the Cypher query language. Suitable for developers exploring connected data.

title: Greenlights
author: Matthew McConaughey
description: Actor Matthew McConaughey shares stories, journal entries and reflections from his life and career. He presents his philosophy of approaching challenges as opportunities. An informal memoir with motivational themes.

title: Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance
author: Angela Duckworth
description: Psychologist Duckworth argues that a combination of passion and sustained persistence, which she calls grit, often predicts achievement better than talent alone. Drawing on her research with cadets, students, spelling contestants and professionals, she explains how grit develops and how parents, teachers and organisations can foster it. Readers interested in motivation, education and long-term goals will find practical, research-based insight.

title: Guns, Germs, and Steel
author: Jared Diamond
description: Diamond asks why societies from Eurasia came to conquer and dominate so much of the world, and argues that the answer lies in geography and environment rather than any innate difference between peoples. Drawing on biology, archaeology and linguistics, he traces how domesticable crops and animals led to farming, dense populations, technology, states and epidemic disease. It suits readers who enjoy sweeping, big-picture world history.

title: Gödel, Escher, Bach
author: Douglas R. Hofstadter
description: Hofstadter explores how meaning and self-awareness might arise from formal systems, weaving together Gödel's incompleteness theorem, Escher's art and Bach's music. Dialogues between characters alternate with chapters on logic, computation and cognition. A long, playful read for those curious about minds, mathematics and AI.

title: HTTP: The Definitive Guide
author: David Gourley
description: A comprehensive reference to the HTTP protocol, covering messages, connections, proxies, caching, gateways, security and content negotiation. It explains how web clients and servers communicate. Useful for web developers and systems engineers.

title: Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution
author: Steven Levy
description: Steven Levy chronicles the programmers and engineers who shaped early computing culture, from MIT in the 1950s to the personal computer pioneers and game developers of the 1980s. The book describes the hacker ethic of sharing and curiosity. A classic history of computing culture.

title: Hacking: The Art of Exploitation
author: Jon Erickson
description: Erickson explains how software exploits really work by grounding the reader first in C programming, assembly and memory layout. From there the chapters move through buffer overflows, format string vulnerabilities, shellcode, network attacks and an introduction to cryptography, with hands-on code to run and debug. Programmers who want a technical, low-level understanding of offensive security will get the most from it.

title: Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow
author: Aurélien Géron
description: Géron offers a practical route into machine learning, beginning with classic techniques in Scikit-Learn such as regression, support vector machines, decision trees, ensembles and clustering. The second half builds deep neural networks with Keras and TensorFlow, covering convolutional and recurrent models, autoencoders and more. Worked examples and notebooks make it well suited to programmers who learn by building.

title: Hatching Twitter
author: Nick Bilton
description: A journalist tells the story of Twitter's founding and early years, focusing on the founders and their conflicts over control of the company. The book shows how personal relationships shaped a major technology firm. A narrative case study of start-up power struggles.

title: Head First Design Patterns
author: Eric Freeman
description: Using a highly visual, conversational style full of diagrams, puzzles and humour, Freeman and his co-authors teach the classic object-oriented design patterns. Readers meet Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Factory, Singleton, Command, Adapter and others through Java examples, alongside the design principles that motivate them. It works well for developers who find conventional pattern catalogues too dry.

title: Head First Java
author: Kathy Sierra
description: A visually rich introduction to Java and object-oriented programming that uses puzzles, diagrams and conversational explanations. It covers classes, inheritance, polymorphism, exceptions, collections and basic GUI and networking topics. Aimed at beginners and students taking a first Java course.

title: Head First SQL
author: Lynn Beighley
description: A visual, conversational introduction to SQL and database design, covering creating tables, writing queries, joins, normalisation and security basics. Puzzles and exercises reinforce learning. Aimed at beginners.

title: High Output Management
author: Andrew S. Grove
description: Andy Grove, former chief executive of Intel, explains management as a production process. He covers meetings, decision-making, planning, performance reviews and training, with an emphasis on a manager's output. A classic guide for new managers, especially in technology.

title: High Performance Browser Networking
author: Ilya Grigorik
description: Ilya Grigorik explains the networking factors that affect web performance, including latency, TCP, TLS, wireless networks, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, WebSocket and WebRTC. He offers practical optimisation advice. Valuable for web developers and engineers.

title: High Performance MySQL
author: Baron Schwartz
description: Written by experienced MySQL consultants, this guide explains how to make MySQL fast and dependable under real workloads. Topics include schema and index design, query optimisation, server configuration, the InnoDB storage engine, replication, scaling strategies and backup and recovery. Database administrators and developers running MySQL in production will find detailed, experience-based advice throughout.

title: Hiroshima
author: John Hersey
description: John Hersey's report on the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, told through the experiences of six survivors. Originally published in 1946, later editions add what happened to them in the following decades. A landmark of journalism and an important historical record.

title: History of the Peloponnesian War
author: Thucydides
description: Thucydides' account of the long war between Athens and Sparta in the fifth century BC, written by an Athenian general who lived through it. It includes speeches, battles and analysis of political decisions. A foundational text in history and international relations.

title: Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products
author: Nir Eyal
description: Eyal sets out a four-stage model of trigger, action, variable reward and investment to explain why some products become part of users' daily routines. Examples from well-known apps and web services illustrate each stage, and a closing section considers the ethics of designing for habit. Product managers, designers and founders are the main audience.

title: How I Built This
author: Guy Raz
description: Based on the podcast of the same name, Guy Raz draws lessons from interviews with founders of well-known companies. Chapters follow the stages of building a business, from finding an idea to growth and setbacks. Accessible and encouraging for new entrepreneurs.

title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
author: Dale Carnegie
description: Carnegie presents practical principles for getting along with people, earning their goodwill, persuading them and leading them without causing resentment. Each idea is illustrated with anecdotes about public figures and ordinary people, emphasising genuine interest, appreciation and seeing things from another's point of view. Readers looking to improve everyday communication at work or at home will find it approachable.

title: Human Compatible
author: Stuart Russell
description: Stuart Russell, co-author of a leading AI textbook, argues that AI systems should be designed to be uncertain about human objectives and to defer to people. He explains risks from misaligned AI and proposes a new approach. Important reading on AI safety.

title: I Am Malala
author: Malala Yousafzai
description: Written with journalist Christina Lamb, Yousafzai's memoir describes her childhood in Pakistan's Swat Valley, where her father ran a school and she spoke out for girls' right to education. She recounts life under growing Taliban control, the attack on her as a schoolgirl and her recovery abroad. It suits readers interested in human rights, education and modern Pakistan.

title: I Will Teach You to Be Rich
author: Ramit Sethi
description: A six-week programme for young adults on managing money, covering credit cards, bank accounts, automated saving, conscious spending and low-cost investing. Sethi focuses on systems that run with little effort. Aimed at students and early-career earners starting to take control of their finances.

title: IPv6 Essentials
author: Silvia Hagen
description: An introduction to IPv6, the newer internet protocol, covering addressing, packet structure, ICMPv6, neighbour discovery, security, routing and transition from IPv4. Useful for engineers planning IPv6 deployments.

title: Ikigai
author: Héctor García
description: An introduction to the Japanese idea of ikigai, a sense of purpose that gives each day meaning. The authors draw on interviews with long-lived residents of Okinawa to discuss routines, diet, community and work. A short, gentle read for anyone thinking about balance and purpose.

title: In Cold Blood
author: Truman Capote
description: Capote reconstructs the murder of a farming family in Holcomb, Kansas, and follows the two drifters responsible, the investigation that tracked them down and the long legal process that followed. Built from extensive interviews and told with the techniques of a novel, it helped shape the modern true crime genre. Readers interested in crime, justice and narrative non-fiction will find it absorbing.

title: India After Gandhi
author: Ramachandra Guha
description: Guha's history of the Republic of India from independence in 1947 onwards. It covers the drafting of the Constitution, the integration of states, wars, political movements, economic change and the challenges of a diverse democracy. A key text for understanding modern India.

title: Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion
author: Robert B. Cialdini
description: Cialdini identifies six principles that drive compliance: reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority and scarcity. Drawing on experimental research and his own time observing salespeople, fundraisers and advertisers, he shows how each one works and how to recognise it being used against you. It appeals to readers in marketing and sales as well as anyone curious about persuasion.

title: Inspired: How to Create Tech Products Customers Love
author: Marty Cagan
description: Marty Cagan explains how leading technology companies discover and build successful products. He covers the role of product managers, empowered teams, product discovery techniques and company culture. A standard reference for product managers and founders.

title: Interconnections
author: Radia Perlman
description: Radia Perlman, inventor of the spanning tree protocol, explains how bridges, switches and routers work and the trade-offs in their design. She covers addressing, routing algorithms and network protocols. A respected reference for network engineers.

title: Internetworking with TCP/IP
author: Douglas E. Comer
description: Douglas Comer's textbook on the principles, protocols and architecture of the TCP/IP internet. It explains addressing, routing, IP, TCP, UDP and higher-level services. Used in university networking courses.

title: Into Thin Air
author: Jon Krakauer
description: A journalist's first-hand account of the 1996 Mount Everest disaster, in which several climbers died during a storm. Krakauer describes the commercial guided expeditions, the climb and the decisions made under extreme conditions. A gripping work of narrative non-fiction about risk and responsibility.

title: Into the Wild
author: Jon Krakauer
description: Krakauer investigates the story of Christopher McCandless, a young college graduate who gave away his savings, travelled across America under an assumed name and walked alone into the Alaskan wilderness. Interviews, letters and journal entries reconstruct his journey, while the author reflects on his own risky climbing ventures. It suits readers drawn to adventure, idealism and questions about why people seek isolation.

title: Introduction to Algorithms
author: Thomas H. Cormen
description: Widely used in university courses, Cormen and his co-authors provide a comprehensive treatment of algorithms and data structures. Coverage ranges from sorting, hashing and trees to graph algorithms, dynamic programming, greedy methods, amortised analysis and NP-completeness, all presented with pseudocode and rigorous analysis. Students and practising engineers use it both as a textbook and as a long-term reference.

title: Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation
author: John E. Hopcroft
description: A classic textbook on the theory of computation, covering finite automata, regular expressions, context-free grammars, pushdown automata, Turing machines, decidability and complexity. Proofs are presented with examples and exercises. Used in theory of computation and compiler foundation courses.

title: Introduction to Computing Systems
author: Yale N. Patt
description: A bottom-up introduction to computing that starts with bits and transistors and progresses through logic circuits, a simple computer architecture, machine and assembly language, and finally C programming. It helps students see how high-level code maps to hardware. Commonly used in first computer engineering courses.

title: Introduction to the Theory of Computation
author: Michael Sipser
description: Sipser introduces the mathematical foundations of computer science in three parts: automata and formal languages, computability and complexity. Readers work through finite automata, regular expressions, context-free grammars, Turing machines, decidability and classes such as P and NP. Clear explanations of proofs make it a common choice for undergraduate and early graduate theory courses.

title: Irrational Exuberance
author: Robert J. Shiller
description: A Nobel-winning economist examines speculative bubbles in stock, bond and housing markets. Shiller combines historical data with psychological and cultural factors to explain why prices can drift far from fundamentals. Relevant to students of economics, finance and market behaviour.

title: JavaScript: The Good Parts
author: Douglas Crockford
description: Crockford argues that JavaScript contains a reliable, expressive subset hidden among its poorly designed features. In a compact format he covers functions, closures, objects, prototypal inheritance, arrays and regular expressions, and lists the parts of the language he recommends avoiding. Developers who already know some JavaScript and want to write cleaner, safer code will benefit most.

title: Joe Celko's SQL for Smarties
author: Joe Celko
description: A collection of advanced SQL techniques for solving difficult problems, such as handling hierarchies, temporal data and complex aggregations. Celko emphasises thinking in sets. Suitable for experienced SQL programmers.

title: Killers of the Flower Moon
author: David Grann
description: Grann investigates a series of murders of members of the Osage Nation in Oklahoma in the 1920s, after oil was found on their land. The book also covers the early FBI's role in the investigation. A detailed work of historical true crime.

title: Kitchen Confidential
author: Anthony Bourdain
description: Chef Anthony Bourdain describes life behind the scenes in restaurant kitchens, from his early jobs to running a New York brasserie. He writes candidly about the culture, pressures and personalities of the trade. A lively memoir for readers interested in food and work.

title: Kubernetes: Up and Running
author: Kelsey Hightower
description: An introduction to Kubernetes, the open-source system for deploying and managing containerised applications. Written by early contributors to the project, it covers pods, services, deployments, storage and operating clusters. Practical for developers and operations engineers.

title: Lab Girl
author: Hope Jahren
description: Geobotanist Hope Jahren combines memoir with writing about trees, seeds and soil. She describes building research laboratories and her partnership with a long-time colleague. A personal view of scientific life for students and general readers.

title: Leaders Eat Last
author: Simon Sinek
description: Sinek explores why some teams build deep trust and cooperation while others do not. Drawing on biology, military examples and business cases, he argues that leaders create safety by putting their people first. Aimed at managers and those interested in organisational culture.

title: Lean Analytics
author: Alistair Croll
description: Croll and Yoskovitz explain how start-ups can use data to measure progress and make decisions. They introduce the idea of focusing on one metric that matters at each stage and give benchmarks for different business models. Practical for founders and growth teams.

title: Learning MySQL
author: Seyed M. M. Tahaghoghi
description: A practical guide to MySQL covering installation, SQL queries, database design, user management, backups and performance basics. Suitable for beginners who want to use MySQL in applications.

title: Learning SQL
author: Alan Beaulieu
description: A beginner's guide to SQL covering queries, filtering, joins, grouping, subqueries, transactions, indexes and views. Examples use a sample database. Suitable for students and developers new to relational databases.

title: Leonardo da Vinci
author: Walter Isaacson
description: Drawing heavily on Leonardo's surviving notebooks, Isaacson portrays the Renaissance figure as painter, engineer, anatomist and relentless observer of nature. The biography links his scientific curiosity to works such as the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and also examines his unfinished projects and personal life. Readers interested in art history, creativity or the connection between art and science will enjoy it.

title: Liar's Poker
author: Michael Lewis
description: Michael Lewis recounts his years as a bond salesman at Salomon Brothers in the 1980s. The memoir describes trading floor culture, the rise of mortgage bonds and the excesses of Wall Street at the time. A readable introduction to how investment banks operated.

title: Life 3.0
author: Max Tegmark
description: Max Tegmark considers how artificial intelligence could change work, law, warfare and society, and what kind of future humanity should aim for. He discusses both near-term issues and long-term possibilities. An accessible introduction to debates about AI.

title: Life of Pi
author: Yann Martel
description: Pi Patel, the son of a zookeeper in Pondicherry, survives a shipwreck only to find himself adrift in a lifeboat with a Bengal tiger. Martel's novel follows his long struggle to stay alive on the Pacific while exploring faith, storytelling and the stories people choose to believe. It appeals to readers who like adventure combined with philosophical questions.

title: Limitless
author: Jim Kwik
description: Jim Kwik presents methods for improving learning, focus and memory, organised around mindset, motivation and methods. The book includes exercises for reading faster and remembering more. Aimed at students and lifelong learners.

title: Linux Basics for Hackers
author: OccupyTheWeb
description: An introduction to Linux for aspiring security professionals, covering the command line, file system, permissions, processes, networking, scripting and anonymity tools on Kali Linux. Suitable for beginners.

title: Linux Network Administrator's Guide
author: Tony Bautts
description: A practical guide to configuring networking on Linux systems, covering TCP/IP setup, name services, firewalls, email, NFS and other common services. Useful for system administrators.

title: Long Walk to Freedom
author: Nelson Mandela
description: Mandela's autobiography traces his life from a rural childhood in the Transkei to legal practice in Johannesburg and leadership in the African National Congress. He describes the struggle against apartheid, his trial, decades of imprisonment including years on Robben Island, and the negotiations that ended white minority rule. It offers a first-hand account of South African history and political conviction.

title: Lord of the Flies
author: William Golding
description: After a plane crash leaves a group of British schoolboys stranded on an uninhabited island, they try to organise themselves with rules and an elected leader. Tensions between Ralph and Jack grow as order gives way to fear and violence. Golding's novel is widely studied for what it suggests about human nature, power and the fragility of civilisation.

title: Losing My Virginity
author: Richard Branson
description: Richard Branson's autobiography covers his early ventures, the founding of Virgin Records and Virgin Atlantic, and his many business adventures. He describes risks, failures and successes in an informal style. An entertaining story of entrepreneurship.

title: Lost Connections
author: Johann Hari
description: Johann Hari investigates causes of depression and anxiety beyond brain chemistry, including disconnection from meaningful work, other people and values. He discusses research and possible ways to reconnect. A personal and journalistic exploration of mental health.

title: Machine Learning
author: Tom M. Mitchell
description: Tom Mitchell's classic textbook introducing the main approaches to machine learning, including concept learning, decision trees, neural networks, Bayesian learning, instance-based learning and reinforcement learning. Clear and concise for students.

title: Machine Learning Yearning
author: Andrew Ng
description: Ng offers practical guidance on the strategic decisions behind machine learning projects rather than on algorithms or code. Short chapters cover setting up development and test sets, choosing a single evaluation metric, error analysis, diagnosing bias and variance, comparing against human-level performance and deciding when end-to-end learning makes sense. It suits engineers and team leads who already know the basics.

title: Machine Learning: A Probabilistic Perspective
author: Kevin P. Murphy
description: A comprehensive textbook presenting machine learning through probabilistic models, covering Bayesian methods, graphical models, Gaussian processes, mixture models and deep learning foundations. Intended for advanced students and researchers.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip Heath
description: The Heath brothers examine why some ideas are remembered and others forgotten. They propose six principles, including simplicity, unexpectedness and stories, for making messages memorable. Useful for teachers, marketers, managers and anyone who needs to communicate clearly.

title: Make Your Bed
author: William H. McRaven
description: A retired US Navy admiral expands a well-known commencement speech into ten lessons drawn from SEAL training and military service. Each chapter links a small habit or experience to resilience, teamwork and perseverance. Brief and anecdotal, aimed at general readers and graduates.

title: Man's Search for Meaning
author: Viktor E. Frankl
description: Frankl, a psychiatrist, recounts his experiences as a prisoner in Nazi concentration camps, including Auschwitz, and reflects on how inmates coped with extreme suffering. The second part outlines logotherapy, his approach to psychotherapy built on the idea that the search for meaning is a central human drive. Readers interested in psychology, philosophy and resilience often return to it.

title: Mastering Bitcoin
author: Andreas M. Antonopoulos
description: A technical guide to how Bitcoin works, covering keys and addresses, wallets, transactions, the blockchain, mining and the peer-to-peer network. It includes code examples for developers. Suitable for programmers and students who want to understand cryptocurrency in depth.

title: Mastery
author: Robert Greene
