description: Robert Greene studies the lives of historical and contemporary masters to describe the path to excellence in a field. He covers finding one's calling, apprenticeship, mentorship and creative work. A long, detailed guide for anyone pursuing a serious craft.

title: Measure What Matters
author: John Doerr
description: Doerr explains objectives and key results, the goal-setting method he learned from Andy Grove at Intel and later introduced to Google. Case studies from companies and non-profits show how OKRs help organisations focus, align teams, track progress and set ambitious targets, and the book also covers ongoing conversations, feedback and recognition. Managers, founders and team leads are the intended readers.

title: Metasploit: The Penetration Tester's Guide
author: David Kennedy
description: Kennedy and his co-authors show how to use the Metasploit Framework to carry out authorised penetration tests. The chapters move from intelligence gathering and vulnerability scanning through exploitation, Meterpreter post-exploitation, client-side and social engineering attacks, to writing custom modules. It is aimed at security professionals and students who want structured, practical experience with the tool.

title: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success
author: Carol S. Dweck
description: Dweck contrasts a fixed mindset, which treats ability as unchangeable, with a growth mindset, which sees skills as something developed through effort and learning. Drawing on her psychological research, she shows how these beliefs affect achievement in school, sport, business, parenting and relationships. Teachers, parents, managers and anyone hoping to handle setbacks differently will find it useful.

title: Misbehaving
author: Richard H. Thaler
description: Richard Thaler tells the story of how behavioural economics developed, as he and others challenged the assumption that people always act rationally. He explains key ideas such as mental accounting and the endowment effect. An accessible history of the field.

title: Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)
author: Carol Tavris
description: Two social psychologists explain cognitive dissonance and how it leads people to justify bad decisions rather than admit mistakes. Examples come from politics, law, medicine and personal relationships. An engaging introduction to self-justification.

title: Mistborn: The Final Empire
author: Brandon Sanderson
description: In a world where ash falls from the sky and an immortal emperor has ruled for a thousand years, a young street thief named Vin is drawn into a crew planning an audacious heist against him. Sanderson builds the story around Allomancy, a magic system in which people draw powers from ingested metals. Fantasy readers who enjoy intricate magic and caper plots will appreciate it.

title: Modern Operating Systems
author: Andrew S. Tanenbaum
description: A widely used textbook on how operating systems work, covering processes and threads, memory management, file systems, input/output, deadlocks, virtualisation and security. Case studies of Linux, Android and Windows connect the theory to real systems. Intended for undergraduate operating systems courses.

title: Money: Master the Game
author: Tony Robbins
description: Tony Robbins condenses interviews with prominent investors into a seven-step plan for personal financial freedom. Topics include saving, fees, asset allocation, retirement income and avoiding common mistakes. Written for general readers who want a broad overview of personal investing.

title: Moneyball
author: Michael Lewis
description: Lewis follows the Oakland Athletics baseball team as its general manager uses statistical analysis to compete with wealthier clubs. The book shows how overlooked data revealed undervalued players. Of interest to readers in sports, data analysis and management.

title: MongoDB in Action
author: Kyle Banker
description: A practical guide to MongoDB covering document modelling, queries, indexing, aggregation, replication and sharding. Examples show how to build applications on the database. Suited to developers new to document databases.

title: MongoDB: The Definitive Guide
author: Kristina Chodorow
description: Chodorow provides a thorough introduction to MongoDB and its document-oriented data model. Readers learn to create, query and update documents, design indexes, use the aggregation framework, and manage replica sets, sharding and day-to-day administration. Developers building applications on MongoDB and administrators responsible for running it in production are the main audience.

title: Napoleon: A Life
author: Andrew Roberts
description: Andrew Roberts uses Napoleon's letters to present a comprehensive biography of the French emperor, from his Corsican childhood to his military campaigns, reforms and final exile. The book assesses both his achievements and his failures. Suited to readers interested in European history.

title: Natural Language Processing with Python
author: Steven Bird
description: An introduction to natural language processing using Python and the Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK). It covers accessing text corpora, tokenisation, tagging, classification, parsing and semantics. Suitable for students in linguistics and computing.

title: Network Programmability and Automation
author: Jason Edelman
description: A practical introduction to automating network operations using Linux, Python, data formats, templates, APIs and tools like Ansible and Git. Written for network engineers moving towards software-driven networking.

title: Network Security Essentials
author: William Stallings
description: Stallings surveys the main tools and protocols used to protect networks and data. Coverage includes symmetric and public-key cryptography, authentication and key distribution, transport-layer and wireless security, email security, IP security, intrusion detection, malware and firewalls. Organised as a textbook, it suits students in networking or security courses as well as practitioners wanting a structured overview.

title: Network Warrior
author: Gary A. Donahue
description: Donahue draws on years of field experience to explain how enterprise networks behave in practice rather than for certification exams. Topics include switching, routing, VLANs, spanning tree, routing protocols, firewalls, quality of service and the Cisco equipment commonly found in data centres. Network engineers moving from study into real-world jobs will find it a practical companion.

title: Networking All-in-One For Dummies
author: Doug Lowe
description: A broad reference covering how to plan, set up and manage computer networks, including hardware, Windows and Linux servers, wireless networks, security and cloud services. Written in an approachable style for beginners and small-office administrators.

title: Neuromancer
author: William Gibson
description: Case, a burned-out hacker no longer able to access cyberspace, is hired by a mysterious employer for one last job alongside the augmented mercenary Molly. Gibson's novel moves from Chiba City to orbital colonies as the crew becomes entangled with powerful artificial intelligences. A foundational work of cyberpunk, it suits readers of science fiction about technology, corporations and virtual worlds.

title: Never Split the Difference
author: Chris Voss
description: A former FBI hostage negotiator presents negotiation techniques based on tactical empathy, active listening and calibrated questions. Chris Voss illustrates each method with stories from crisis negotiations. Useful for business negotiations and everyday conversations.

title: Nickel and Dimed
author: Barbara Ehrenreich
description: Ehrenreich takes a series of low-wage jobs in the United States, including waitressing, cleaning and retail work, to see whether she can live on the pay. She describes the physical demands, costs of housing and daily pressures workers face. A well-known piece of immersive reporting on poverty and work.

title: Night
author: Elie Wiesel
description: Elie Wiesel's memoir of his experiences as a teenager in the Nazi concentration camps of Auschwitz and Buchenwald with his father. It is a short, direct account of the Holocaust and its effect on faith and humanity. Widely read in schools and universities.

title: No Rules Rules
author: Reed Hastings
description: Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings and business professor Erin Meyer describe the company's culture of freedom and responsibility. They explain practices such as high talent density, candid feedback and minimal rules on expenses and holidays. A look at an unconventional management approach.

title: Nudge
author: Richard H. Thaler
description: An economist and a legal scholar explain how the way choices are presented, or choice architecture, influences decisions about health, money and happiness. They argue for designing choices that help people while preserving freedom. Influential in behavioural economics and public policy.

title: On Writing
author: Stephen King
description: Stephen King combines a memoir of his development as a writer with practical advice on the craft. He discusses vocabulary, grammar, style, revision and the habits of a working writer. Helpful for aspiring writers and readers interested in how fiction is made.

title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin
description: Charles Darwin's 1859 work presenting the theory of evolution by natural selection, supported by observations from nature, breeding and fossils. It reshaped biology and our understanding of life. A foundational scientific text for students of biology.

title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
author: Gabriel García Márquez
description: García Márquez follows seven generations of the Buendía family in Macondo, a fictional Colombian town that grows from an isolated settlement into a place shaken by civil war and foreign commerce. Everyday life and the miraculous sit side by side in this landmark of magical realism. Readers who enjoy rich, multigenerational storytelling and Latin American literature will find much to explore.

title: One Up On Wall Street
author: Peter Lynch
description: Lynch, who managed Fidelity's Magellan Fund, argues that ordinary investors can spot promising companies through products and businesses they encounter in daily life. He sorts stocks into categories such as slow growers, stalwarts, fast growers, cyclicals, turnarounds and asset plays, and explains how to research each before buying. It suits individual investors wanting a practical approach to choosing stocks.

title: Operating System Concepts
author: Abraham Silberschatz
description: Silberschatz and his co-authors present the core ideas behind modern operating systems in a widely adopted course text. Chapters cover processes and threads, CPU scheduling, synchronisation, deadlocks, memory and virtual memory, file systems, storage, protection and security, with examples drawn from Linux, Windows and other systems. Computer science students and developers wanting conceptual grounding will benefit.

title: Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives
author: John C. Hull
description: A standard textbook on derivative securities, covering futures, forwards, swaps, options, pricing models such as Black-Scholes, and risk management. It balances theory with market practice and numerical methods. Widely used in finance degree programmes and by practitioners.

title: Outliers
author: Malcolm Gladwell
description: Gladwell argues that exceptional success depends less on individual talent than on opportunity, timing, cultural background and accumulated practice. Case studies range from the birth months of professional hockey players to the Beatles, software pioneers and the role of cultural habits in airline safety. Readers who enjoy accessible social science and counterintuitive explanations will find it engaging.

title: Outwitting the Devil
author: Napoleon Hill
description: Written in 1938 but published decades later, this book by Napoleon Hill presents an imagined conversation about fear, procrastination and habits that hold people back. Annotated editions add modern commentary. A classic of motivational literature.

title: Pale Blue Dot
author: Carl Sagan
description: Sagan reflects on humanity's place in the universe, inspired by the photograph of Earth taken by Voyager 1 from billions of kilometres away. The book surveys planetary exploration and considers the future of human space travel. A thoughtful work of popular astronomy.

title: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning
author: Christopher M. Bishop
description: Bishop presents machine learning from a probabilistic and largely Bayesian perspective. The text covers probability distributions, linear models for regression and classification, neural networks, kernel methods and support vector machines, graphical models, mixture models and expectation maximisation, approximate inference and sampling methods. Its mathematical depth makes it best suited to graduate students and researchers comfortable with calculus and linear algebra.

title: Penetration Testing
author: Georgia Weidman
description: Georgia Weidman provides a hands-on introduction to penetration testing, covering setting up a lab, information gathering, exploitation, password attacks, web and wireless testing, and post-exploitation. Suited to beginners in ethical hacking.

title: PostgreSQL: Up and Running
author: Regina O. Obe
description: Obe and Hsu give a concise, practical tour of PostgreSQL for people who need to get productive quickly. Readers learn installation and administration, the psql and pgAdmin tools, data types, advanced SQL features, writing functions, query tuning and replication. Developers and administrators coming from other databases, or new to PostgreSQL, will find it a compact starting point.

title: Postwar
author: Tony Judt
description: A comprehensive history of Europe from the end of the Second World War in 1945 to the early twenty-first century. Judt covers both Western and Eastern Europe, including reconstruction, the Cold War, the fall of communism and European integration. A detailed reference for students of modern history.

title: Practical Malware Analysis
author: Michael Sikorski
description: Sikorski and Honig teach the techniques used to dissect malicious software, from basic static and dynamic analysis to disassembly and debugging with tools such as IDA Pro and OllyDbg. Later chapters address Windows internals, anti-disassembly and anti-debugging tricks, and packed code. Hands-on labs with real samples make it valuable for aspiring malware analysts and incident responders.

title: Practical Packet Analysis
author: Chris Sanders
description: Sanders shows how to capture and interpret network traffic using Wireshark. After explaining how packet sniffing works, he walks through common protocols such as TCP, IP, DNS and HTTP, then applies these skills to troubleshooting slow networks, investigating security incidents and examining wireless traffic. Network administrators, support staff and security beginners will find it a practical introduction.

title: Practical SQL
author: Anthony DeBarros
description: A beginner-friendly introduction to SQL using PostgreSQL and real public datasets. It covers queries, joins, statistics, text and geographic data. Suitable for data journalists, analysts and students.

title: Predictably Irrational
author: Dan Ariely
description: Ariely uses inventive experiments to show that people make irrational decisions in consistent, predictable ways. Chapters explore relative comparisons, anchoring, the pull of free offers, the clash between social and market norms, procrastination, ownership and dishonesty. Written in an accessible style, it appeals to readers curious about behavioural economics and the hidden forces behind everyday choices.

title: Prediction Machines
author: Ajay Agrawal
description: Three economists explain AI as a technology that makes prediction cheap, and show how this changes decision-making, jobs and business strategy. Useful for managers and students of business and economics.

title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
description: Elizabeth Bennet, the sharp-witted second of five daughters in a family of modest means, clashes with the proud and wealthy Mr Darcy in Regency-era England. Austen's novel examines marriage, money, social class and the danger of judging too quickly, with much of its humour coming from dialogue and character. It suits readers who enjoy classic romance and social comedy.

title: Pro Git
author: Scott Chacon
description: A comprehensive guide to the Git version control system, covering basic commands, branching, remote repositories, collaboration workflows and Git's internals. Written by members of the Git community. Useful for beginners and experienced developers alike.

title: Probabilistic Graphical Models
author: Daphne Koller
description: A detailed textbook on representing and reasoning with uncertainty using Bayesian networks and Markov networks. It covers representation, inference and learning. Aimed at graduate students and researchers.

title: Programming Pearls
author: Jon Bentley
description: Bentley gathers essays on the craft of programming, focusing on how careful problem definition and clever thinking lead to simple, efficient solutions. Topics include algorithm design, back-of-the-envelope estimates, data structures, verifying correctness, code tuning, sorting, searching and sampling, each supported by exercises. Working programmers who want to sharpen their problem-solving skills will benefit most.

title: Psycho-Cybernetics
author: Maxwell Maltz
description: A plastic surgeon's account of how self-image influences behaviour and how it can be changed through visualisation and mental rehearsal. Maltz combines observations from his patients with exercises for goal setting and confidence. A foundational text for many later self-help programmes.

title: Purple Cow
author: Seth Godin
description: Godin argues that traditional advertising is less effective and that products must be genuinely remarkable to stand out. The book gives examples of companies that built remarkable products and offers ideas for doing the same. A short read for marketers and entrepreneurs.

title: Python Crash Course
author: Eric Matthes
description: Matthes teaches Python from the ground up, beginning with variables, lists, dictionaries, loops, functions, classes, files and testing. The second half applies these skills in three projects: an arcade-style game built with Pygame, data visualisations, and a web application using Django. Complete beginners and those switching from another language will find a clear, project-based path.

title: Python Data Science Handbook
author: Jake VanderPlas
description: A practical reference to the core Python data science stack: IPython, NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib and scikit-learn. It shows how to clean, analyse and visualise data and build machine learning models. Suitable for students and analysts.

title: Python Machine Learning
author: Sebastian Raschka
description: Raschka combines machine learning theory with working Python code, explaining how algorithms operate before showing how to apply them with libraries such as scikit-learn and TensorFlow. Coverage runs from classifiers, preprocessing and model evaluation through ensembles, regression and clustering to neural networks and deep learning. It suits readers with some Python experience who want both intuition and implementation.

title: Quiet: The Power of Introverts
author: Susan Cain
description: Cain examines how modern Western culture came to favour outgoing, talkative personalities and what is lost when introverts are overlooked. Drawing on psychology, neuroscience and interviews, she looks at schools, workplaces and relationships, and offers suggestions for introverts and the people who work or live with them. Readers who identify as quiet, or who manage or teach them, will find it relevant.

title: Radical Candor
author: Kim Scott
description: A former technology executive presents a framework for managers based on caring personally while challenging directly. Scott gives practical advice on giving and receiving feedback, building relationships and guiding teams. Helpful for new and experienced managers.

title: Ready Player One
author: Ernest Cline
description: In a bleak near future, teenager Wade Watts spends most of his life inside the OASIS, a vast virtual reality world. When its creator dies and leaves a fortune hidden behind a series of puzzles, Wade joins a global hunt that leans heavily on 1980s films, games and music, while a powerful corporation competes for the prize. Fans of fast-paced science fiction and pop culture will enjoy it.

title: Redis in Action
author: Josiah L. Carlson
description: Carlson teaches Redis through realistic application problems rather than abstract reference material. After introducing strings, lists, sets, hashes and sorted sets, he builds features such as caching, session storage, counters, search, job queues and messaging, then covers persistence, replication, sharding and Lua scripting. Developers looking to use Redis beyond simple caching will find it practical.

title: Refactoring
author: Martin Fowler
description: Fowler explains how to improve the structure of existing code through small, behaviour-preserving changes backed by tests. Alongside guidance on recognising code smells and deciding when to refactor, the book provides a detailed catalogue of named refactorings with motivation, mechanics and examples in JavaScript. Professional developers working on long-lived codebases will find it a lasting reference.

title: Refactoring Databases
author: Scott W. Ambler
description: Ambler and Sadalage describe techniques for evolving a database schema safely through small, tested changes. The book catalogues refactorings for structure, data quality and referential integrity. Useful for teams practising agile development.

title: Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction
author: Richard S. Sutton
description: Sutton and Barto present the foundations of reinforcement learning, in which an agent learns to act by interacting with an environment and receiving rewards. Chapters cover multi-armed bandits, Markov decision processes, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo methods, temporal-difference learning, function approximation and policy gradient methods, with links to psychology and neuroscience. It serves students and researchers as the standard introduction to the field.

title: Release It!
author: Michael T. Nygard
description: A guide to designing and deploying software that survives real-world production conditions. Nygard describes stability patterns such as timeouts and circuit breakers, along with common failure modes and operational practices. Valuable for developers building online systems.

title: Relentless
author: Tim S. Grover
description: Tim Grover, a trainer of elite athletes including Michael Jordan, describes the mindset he believes separates great performers from good ones. The book focuses on drive, discipline and handling pressure. Direct reading for athletes and competitive people.

title: Rework
author: Jason Fried
description: The founders of the software company 37signals offer short essays challenging conventional business advice. They argue for staying small, avoiding unnecessary meetings and planning, and launching early. A quick, opinionated read for founders and small teams.

title: Rich Dad Poor Dad
author: Robert T. Kiyosaki
description: Kiyosaki contrasts the money habits of his highly educated father with those of a friend's entrepreneurial father, using the comparison to argue for financial literacy. He stresses the difference between assets and liabilities, building income that does not depend on a salary, and thinking like an owner or investor. Readers beginning to think about personal finance often use it as a motivational starting point.

title: Routing TCP/IP
author: Jeff Doyle
description: A detailed guide to interior routing protocols, including RIP, EIGRP, OSPF and IS-IS, with configuration examples on Cisco routers. It explains how routing protocols work and how to troubleshoot them. Useful for network engineers and certification candidates.

title: Running Lean
author: Ash Maurya
description: Ash Maurya presents a systematic method for testing a business idea before investing heavily in it. The book introduces the Lean Canvas and explains how to identify risky assumptions, interview customers and measure progress. A hands-on guide for founders and product teams.

title: SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome
author: Mary Beard
description: Beard tells the story of Rome from its legendary origins to the early third century CE, when citizenship was extended across the empire. She examines how historians know what they know, questions familiar myths, and gives attention to ordinary Romans as well as emperors and senators. General readers wanting a thoughtful, up-to-date account of Roman history will find it rewarding.

title: SQL Antipatterns
author: Bill Karwin
description: Bill Karwin describes common mistakes in database design and SQL queries, such as storing lists in a single column, and explains why they cause problems. Each antipattern comes with better solutions. Practical for developers working with relational databases.

title: SQL Performance Explained
author: Markus Winand
description: Winand explains database indexing from a developer's perspective, showing how B-tree indexes work and how to write SQL that uses them well. Topics include where clauses, multi-column indexes, functions, joins, sorting, grouping, fetching partial results and the cost of writes, with examples across Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server. Application developers who write SQL will find it short and practical.

title: Sams Teach Yourself SQL in 10 Minutes
author: Ben Forta
description: A compact introduction to SQL organised into short lessons, each designed to be completed quickly. It covers retrieving, sorting, filtering, joining and modifying data across common database systems. Handy as a quick reference.

title: Sandworm
author: Andy Greenberg
description: Andy Greenberg reports on a group of Russian state-backed hackers responsible for attacks on Ukraine's power grid and the NotPetya malware outbreak. He describes the investigators who tracked them. A gripping account of modern cyber warfare.

title: Sapiens
author: Yuval Noah Harari
description: Harari surveys the history of Homo sapiens through a series of revolutions: cognitive, agricultural and scientific. He argues that the human capacity to believe in shared stories such as money, religion, nations and empires allowed large-scale cooperation, and he questions whether progress has made people happier. History readers seeking a broad, provocative overview of the human past will find plenty to discuss.

title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
author: Yuval Noah Harari
description: Ranging across biology, anthropology and economics, Harari asks how a once-insignificant ape came to dominate the planet. Central ideas include the role of collective fictions in organising society, the mixed consequences of farming, the unifying power of money and empire, and the rise of modern science and capitalism. It suits curious non-specialists who enjoy big questions and debate-provoking arguments.

title: Sapiens: A Graphic History
author: Yuval Noah Harari
description: Harari's account of early human history is retold here as a graphic novel, created with artist Daniel Casanave and co-writer David Vandermeulen. Through illustrated panels, recurring characters and humour, it follows early humans, the spread of Homo sapiens and its encounters with other species. The format makes the ideas accessible to younger readers and anyone who prefers visual storytelling.

title: Say Nothing
author: Patrick Radden Keefe
description: Using the 1972 disappearance of a mother of ten in Belfast as its starting point, this book examines the Troubles in Northern Ireland. Keefe follows several people involved in the conflict and its long aftermath. A carefully researched account of political violence and memory.

title: Secrets and Lies
author: Bruce Schneier
description: Bruce Schneier explains why security is a process rather than a product, covering threats, attacks, cryptography, networks and human factors. He argues for thinking about systems as a whole. Accessible to managers and technical readers.

title: Secrets of Sand Hill Road
author: Scott Kupor
description: A venture capitalist explains how venture capital firms raise funds, choose investments and structure deals. Kupor covers term sheets, board dynamics and exits from the founder's perspective. Valuable for entrepreneurs seeking investment.

title: Security Analysis
author: Benjamin Graham
description: The foundational text of value investing, explaining how to analyse bonds and stocks using financial statements and a margin of safety. Later editions include commentary from modern investors relating the ideas to current markets. A demanding reference for serious students of finance.

title: Security Engineering
author: Ross Anderson
description: Ross Anderson's broad guide to building systems that remain dependable in the face of error and malice. It covers cryptography, access control, protocols, banking, hardware, psychology and policy. A comprehensive reference for security students and practitioners.

title: Serious Cryptography
author: Jean-Philippe Aumasson
description: A practical introduction to modern cryptography, explaining how algorithms such as AES, hash functions, RSA and elliptic curves work and how they can fail. It avoids heavy mathematics while staying precise. Suitable for developers and security students.

title: Seven Databases in Seven Weeks
author: Eric Redmond
description: Redmond and Wilson guide readers through seven different databases, including PostgreSQL, Riak, HBase, MongoDB, CouchDB, Neo4j and Redis, spending a few focused sessions on each. Comparing relational, key-value, column, document and graph models shows the trade-offs each design makes. Developers and architects choosing a data store, or wanting to broaden their perspective, will benefit from the hands-on survey.

title: Shoe Dog
author: Phil Knight
description: The memoir of Phil Knight, who started Nike as a small business importing running shoes from Japan. He describes the company's early financial struggles, partnerships and growth. An engaging story of entrepreneurship and persistence.

title: Silent Spring
author: Rachel Carson
description: Carson documents the harm caused by the widespread use of synthetic pesticides such as DDT, tracing their effects on birds, fish, wildlife, soil, water and human health. She challenges indiscriminate spraying and the claims of the chemical industry while explaining the underlying science in accessible prose. Readers interested in ecology, environmental history and public policy will find it highly relevant.

title: Site Reliability Engineering
author: Niall Richard Murphy
description: Engineers from Google describe how the company runs large production systems using a discipline it calls site reliability engineering. Chapters cover service level objectives, error budgets, reducing toil, monitoring, on-call work, incident response, blameless postmortems, release engineering and load balancing. Operations staff, software engineers and managers responsible for reliable services will find concrete practices to adapt.

title: So Good They Can't Ignore You
author: Cal Newport
description: Cal Newport challenges the advice to follow your passion, arguing that valuable skills and career capital matter more for finding satisfying work. He shares examples and practical strategies. Helpful for students choosing careers and early-career professionals.

title: Social Engineering: The Art of Human Hacking
author: Christopher Hadnagy
description: Hadnagy examines how attackers manipulate people rather than machines to gain access to information and systems. He covers information gathering, elicitation, pretexting, psychological principles of influence, body language and the tools used by professional testers, and explains how organisations can defend against these techniques. Security practitioners and anyone responsible for staff awareness training will find it informative.

title: Speech and Language Processing
author: Daniel Jurafsky
description: A leading textbook on natural language processing and speech recognition, covering language models, parsing, semantics, machine translation, dialogue and neural methods. Used in university NLP courses.

title: Sprint
author: Jake Knapp
description: Knapp, with colleagues from Google Ventures, describes a five-day process for answering critical business questions quickly. A small team maps the problem, sketches solutions, decides on the strongest idea, builds a realistic prototype and tests it with real customers by the end of the week. Startup teams, product managers and designers can follow the step-by-step instructions directly.

title: Stalingrad
author: Antony Beevor
description: Beevor's history of the Battle of Stalingrad from 1942 to 1943, one of the turning points of the Second World War. Using archival sources and soldiers' letters, he covers both the strategy and the experiences of soldiers and civilians. A respected work of military history.

title: Start with Why
author: Simon Sinek
description: Sinek argues that inspiring leaders and organisations communicate their purpose, their why, before explaining what they do and how. He illustrates the idea with examples from companies and public figures. A popular read on leadership, communication and motivation.

title: Startup Communities
author: Brad Feld
description: Brad Feld explains how to build a thriving entrepreneurial ecosystem in any city, drawing on his experience in Boulder, Colorado. He argues that entrepreneurs must lead the effort, supported by universities, investors and government. Relevant for founders and community organisers.

title: Steal Like an Artist
author: Austin Kleon
description: A short, illustrated guide to creativity by Austin Kleon. He encourages readers to learn from others' work, collect influences and develop their own voice through practice. Accessible inspiration for students, writers and artists.

title: Steve Jobs
author: Walter Isaacson
description: Based on many interviews with Jobs and the people around him, Isaacson's biography follows the Apple co-founder from his adoption and youth through the founding of Apple, his departure, NeXT and Pixar, and his return. It covers the creation of products such as the iPod and iPhone and presents both his vision and his difficult temperament. Readers interested in technology and business leadership will find it detailed.

title: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs
author: Harold Abelson
description: Originally developed for an introductory course at MIT, Abelson and Sussman use the Scheme language to teach the fundamental ideas of programming. Readers build abstractions with procedures and data, explore higher-order functions, state and streams, write interpreters for new languages and finally model computation at the level of register machines and compilers. It rewards motivated students willing to work through challenging exercises.

title: Stumbling on Happiness
author: Daniel Gilbert
description: Gilbert, a Harvard psychologist, explores why people are surprisingly poor at predicting what will make them happy in the future. Using research from psychology, neuroscience and behavioural economics, he shows how imagination fills in details, projects the present onto the future and underestimates our ability to adapt. Written with humour, it suits general readers curious about happiness and decision-making.

title: Superintelligence
author: Nick Bostrom
description: Nick Bostrom examines what might happen if machines surpass human intelligence, exploring possible paths to superintelligence, its risks and strategies for keeping it aligned with human interests. A central work in debates on AI safety.

title: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!
author: Richard P. Feynman
description: A collection of stories from the life of physicist Richard Feynman, as told to a friend. It covers his curiosity, pranks, work on the Manhattan Project and adventures outside science. An entertaining look at a famous scientist's way of thinking.

title: T-SQL Fundamentals
author: Itzik Ben-Gan
description: An introduction to querying Microsoft SQL Server with Transact-SQL. It covers single-table queries, joins, subqueries, set operators, window functions, data modification and transactions, with an emphasis on set-based thinking. Suitable for beginners.

title: TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1
author: W. Richard Stevens
description: Stevens explains the TCP/IP protocol suite by showing the protocols in action through real packet traces rather than by summarising specifications. Coverage includes the link layer, IP addressing, ARP, ICMP, UDP, DNS and an extended treatment of TCP connection management, timeouts, flow control and congestion control. Network engineers, system programmers and advanced students use it as a detailed reference.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Suite
author: Behrouz A. Forouzan
description: Forouzan explains the TCP/IP protocols layer by layer, including IP addressing, routing, ARP, ICMP, UDP, TCP, DNS and application protocols. Clear diagrams support each topic. Designed for students taking networking courses.

title: Team Topologies
author: Matthew Skelton
description: Skelton and Pais present a model for organising software teams around four team types and three interaction modes. The book links team structure to software architecture and fast delivery. Useful for engineering managers and architects.

title: Team of Rivals
author: Doris Kearns Goodwin
description: Goodwin examines Abraham Lincoln's presidency through his relationships with the men who had competed against him for the 1860 Republican nomination and later served in his cabinet. Drawing on letters and diaries, she shows how Lincoln managed strong personalities during the Civil War. Readers interested in American history, political leadership and group biography will find a detailed, character-driven account.

title: Test Driven Development: By Example
author: Kent Beck
description: Kent Beck demonstrates test-driven development by building code through short cycles of writing a failing test, making it pass and refactoring. Worked examples show the rhythm of the practice, followed by patterns for applying it. A core reference for developers learning TDD.

title: That Will Never Work
author: Marc Randolph
description: Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph recounts how the company began as a DVD-by-mail service and survived its early years. He shares lessons on testing ideas, building a team and handling doubt. An engaging start-up story with practical takeaways.

title: The $100 Startup
author: Chris Guillebeau
description: Guillebeau collects stories of people who built small, profitable businesses with very little starting money, often around skills or interests they already had. The book distils their experiences into practical steps for testing an idea, setting a price, launching quickly and growing without outside funding. It suits aspiring side-hustlers, freelancers and anyone considering self-employment.

title: The 10X Rule
author: Grant Cardone
description: Grant Cardone argues that most people underestimate the effort needed to reach their goals and should set targets and take action at ten times their usual level. The book focuses on ambition, persistence and sales. A high-energy read for driven readers.

title: The 4-Hour Workweek
author: Timothy Ferriss
description: Ferriss challenges the conventional path of working long hours until retirement and proposes designing a life around time and mobility instead. He covers eliminating low-value tasks, outsourcing, automating income through small online businesses and negotiating remote work. Readers curious about productivity shortcuts, lifestyle design and unconventional career choices will find a provocative set of tactics and case examples.

title: The 48 Laws of Power
author: Robert Greene
description: Greene organises lessons about influence, status and manipulation into forty-eight principles, each illustrated with episodes from history involving courtiers, rulers, generals and con artists. The tone is amoral and analytical, describing how power tends to operate rather than how it should. Readers interested in strategy, historical anecdote and the darker side of social dynamics often use it as a study of human behaviour.

title: The 5 AM Club
author: Robin Sharma
description: Told largely as a fable about a mentor and two struggling students, Sharma's book argues for starting the day early with a structured routine. Its core method divides the first hour into periods of exercise, reflection and learning. It is aimed at readers seeking motivation, better habits and a more deliberate approach to personal productivity and wellbeing.

title: The 5 Love Languages
author: Gary Chapman
description: Chapman, a marriage counsellor, proposes that people tend to give and receive affection in five main ways: words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service and physical touch. Misunderstandings arise, he suggests, when partners express love in different ways. Couples and anyone wanting to improve close relationships will find practical examples and exercises for identifying their own preferences.

title: The 5 Second Rule
author: Mel Robbins
description: Mel Robbins describes a simple technique of counting down from five to push oneself into action before hesitation takes over. She applies it to procrastination, confidence and anxiety. A quick, practical read.

title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
author: Stephen R. Covey
description: Covey presents a principle-based framework for personal and professional effectiveness, moving from self-mastery toward cooperation with others. The seven habits include being proactive, beginning with the end in mind, putting first things first and seeking mutual benefit. Widely used in leadership training, it suits readers who want a structured approach to character, priorities and working relationships.

title: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
author: Shoshana Zuboff
description: Zuboff argues that major technology companies have created a new economic model based on collecting and analysing personal data to predict and influence behaviour. She examines the social and political consequences. A substantial work on privacy and the digital economy.

title: The Alchemist
author: Paulo Coelho
description: Coelho tells the story of Santiago, an Andalusian shepherd boy who leaves home after a recurring dream and travels across North Africa toward the Egyptian pyramids in search of treasure. Along the way he meets a king, a merchant and an alchemist who teach him about following one's purpose. Written in a simple parable style, the novel appeals to readers who enjoy philosophical, spiritual fiction.

title: The Algorithm Design Manual
author: Steven S. Skiena
description: Skiena's guide to algorithms combines a practical explanation of design techniques with a large catalogue of common computational problems and approaches for solving them. Real-world war stories show how problems are recognised and modelled in practice. Students, interview candidates and working programmers use it both as a textbook and as a reference for choosing suitable algorithms and data structures.

title: The Alignment Problem
author: Brian Christian
description: Brian Christian explores the challenge of making machine learning systems behave as intended. He covers bias, fairness, transparency, reinforcement learning and learning from human preferences through interviews with researchers. Accessible for general readers.

title: The Anarchy
author: William Dalrymple
description: Dalrymple tells how the East India Company, a private trading business, came to control much of the Indian subcontinent in the eighteenth century. He describes the decline of the Mughal Empire, wars and the Company's growing power. A detailed history of early colonial India.

title: The Annotated Turing
author: Charles Petzold
description: Petzold guides readers line by line through Alan Turing's 1936 paper that introduced the Turing machine. He supplies the mathematical and historical background needed to follow it, along with notes on Turing's life. Useful for students who want to understand the foundations of computation from the original source.

title: The Art of Computer Programming
author: Donald E. Knuth
description: Knuth's multi-volume work offers a rigorous, mathematical treatment of fundamental algorithms, including topics such as information structures, random numbers, arithmetic, sorting and searching. Examples are expressed in an assembly language for a hypothetical machine, and the exercises range from routine to research level. It suits serious students and computer scientists who want deep analytical understanding rather than a quick introduction.

title: The Art of Deception
author: Kevin D. Mitnick
description: Kevin Mitnick, once a well-known hacker, explains how social engineers manipulate people into revealing information or granting access. The book uses scenarios to show common tactics and how organisations can defend against them. Useful for security awareness.

title: The Art of Invisibility
author: Kevin D. Mitnick
description: Mitnick explains how personal data is collected and tracked online and offers practical steps for protecting privacy. Topics include passwords, encryption, browsing, email and mobile devices. Aimed at general readers concerned about privacy.

title: The Art of SQL
author: Stéphane Faroult
description: Stéphane Faroult explains how to write efficient SQL by thinking about how queries interact with database structures. Chapters use military strategy as a theme to discuss design, indexing and query patterns. For developers who want faster, more scalable queries.

title: The Art of War
author: Sun Tzu
description: Attributed to the ancient Chinese general Sun Tzu, this short treatise on military strategy covers planning, deception, terrain, the use of spies and the value of winning without battle. Its compact chapters have long been read outside warfare as lessons in competition and leadership. Business readers often apply its ideas to negotiation, management and market strategy.

title: The Art of the Start
author: Guy Kawasaki
description: Guy Kawasaki offers practical advice for launching a new venture, including positioning, pitching, writing a business plan, recruiting, raising money and building a brand. The tone is direct and lively. Suitable for entrepreneurs in start-ups and non-profits.

title: The Ascent of Money
author: Niall Ferguson
description: A historian traces the development of money, credit, banking, bonds, stocks, insurance and real estate from ancient times to the modern global economy. Ferguson links financial innovations to major historical events. A broad, accessible history for general readers and students.

title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin
description: Franklin recounts his own life, from a modest Boston childhood and printing apprenticeship to success in Philadelphia as a businessman, writer and civic organiser. He describes his methods for self-improvement, including a plan for cultivating thirteen virtues. Left unfinished at his death, the memoir gives readers a first-hand view of colonial American life and an influential model of self-made ambition.

title: The Automatic Millionaire
author: David Bach
description: Bach argues that ordinary earners can build wealth by deciding once and then automating good financial decisions. He recommends paying yourself first through automatic retirement contributions, building an emergency fund and paying down a mortgage and debt systematically. The book suits beginners who want a simple, low-effort savings plan rather than active money management.

title: The Barefoot Investor
author: Scott Pape
description: Pape, an Australian finance columnist, sets out a step-by-step plan for managing household money, from organising bank accounts into buckets to clearing debt, buying a home and preparing for retirement. Advice is framed around Australian accounts and superannuation, though many principles apply elsewhere. Written in a conversational style, it suits individuals and families seeking an uncomplicated money system.

title: The Big Short
author: Michael Lewis
description: Lewis tells the story of a few investors who foresaw the collapse of the US housing market and bet against subprime mortgage bonds before the 2008 financial crisis. The book explains the financial products involved through the people who studied them. An accessible account of how the crisis unfolded.

title: The Blind Watchmaker
author: Richard Dawkins
description: Dawkins explains how natural selection can produce complex living things without a designer. He uses examples and computer simulations to show cumulative selection at work. A popular science classic on evolution.

title: The Body Keeps the Score
author: Bessel van der Kolk
description: Van der Kolk, a psychiatrist, draws on decades of clinical work and research to explain how trauma affects the brain, the body and relationships. He reviews developments in neuroscience and describes a range of treatments, including therapy, yoga, neurofeedback and EMDR. Survivors, clinicians and general readers interested in mental health will find an accessible account of trauma and recovery.

title: The Body: A Guide for Occupants
author: Bill Bryson
description: Bill Bryson tours the human body, explaining how its organs and systems work, how diseases affect it and how medicine has developed. The book is full of facts and stories. Accessible reading for general audiences and students.

title: The Bogleheads' Guide to Investing
author: Taylor Larimore
description: Written by Larimore and co-authors from the online community inspired by Vanguard founder John Bogle, this guide promotes a simple, low-cost approach to investing. Topics include saving early, diversifying with index funds, keeping fees and taxes low, and staying the course through market swings. It suits beginners and do-it-yourself investors who want a clear, long-term plan.

title: The Book Thief
author: Markus Zusak
description: Set in a small town in Nazi Germany, Zusak's novel follows Liesel, a foster girl who steals books and learns to read while her adoptive family hides a Jewish man in their basement. The story is narrated by Death, which gives it an unusual, reflective voice. It suits older teens and adults interested in historical fiction about ordinary lives during the Second World War.

title: The Book of Why
author: Judea Pearl
description: Judea Pearl and Dana Mackenzie explain the science of cause and effect, describing causal diagrams and how they help answer questions that data alone cannot. The book discusses implications for statistics and AI. Accessible reading on causal reasoning.

title: The Boys in the Boat
author: Daniel James Brown
description: The true story of the University of Washington rowing crew, made up largely of working-class young men, who competed at the 1936 Berlin Olympics. Brown focuses on one rower's difficult upbringing alongside the team's development. An inspiring sports history set against the Great Depression.

title: The C Programming Language
author: Brian W. Kernighan
description: Kernighan and Ritchie, the latter one of the language's creators, provide a compact introduction to C covering types, operators, control flow, functions, pointers, structures and input and output. Concise examples and exercises build toward practical programs, and a reference manual appears at the end. Programmers learning C or seeking a precise understanding of the language still use it as a standard text.

title: The Catcher in the Rye
author: J.D. Salinger
description: Holden Caulfield, a teenager expelled from his boarding school, spends several days wandering New York City before returning home to face his parents. Through his restless, sardonic narration, Salinger explores alienation, grief, and the difficulty of growing up in a world Holden sees as false. The novel remains widely studied and suits readers interested in coming-of-age stories and classic American fiction.

title: The Clean Coder
author: Robert C. Martin
description: Martin turns from code quality to the conduct of software developers, discussing what professional behaviour looks like in a programming career. He covers saying no to unrealistic demands, making commitments, estimating, managing time and pressure, testing practices and collaboration. Developers at any stage who want to work more responsibly and communicate better with colleagues and managers will find practical guidance.

title: The Code Book
author: Simon Singh
description: Simon Singh tells the history of codes and ciphers from ancient times to modern public-key cryptography. The book explains how codes were made and broken, including the Enigma machine. Accessible for general readers and students.

title: The Code Breaker
author: Walter Isaacson
description: Isaacson's account of Jennifer Doudna and the development of CRISPR gene editing. The book explains the science, the competition among researchers and the ethical questions raised by editing human genes. Of interest to students of biology and general readers.

title: The Compound Effect
author: Darren Hardy
description: Darren Hardy explains how small, consistent choices and habits add up to large results over time. He offers practical steps for tracking behaviour, building momentum and staying on course. A straightforward guide to steady self-improvement.

title: The Cuckoo's Egg
author: Clifford Stoll
description: An astronomer working as a systems administrator traces a small accounting error to a hacker breaking into US military and research computers in the 1980s. Stoll's account shows early network security investigation in action. A classic true story.

title: The Da Vinci Code
author: Dan Brown
description: Harvard symbologist Robert Langdon is drawn into a murder investigation at the Louvre and, with cryptologist Sophie Neveu, follows a trail of codes hidden in art and history. The chase across France and England involves secret societies and alternative theories about Christian history. Brown's fast-paced thriller suits readers who enjoy puzzles, conspiracies and short, cliffhanger chapters.

title: The Daily Stoic
author: Ryan Holiday
description: A year of daily readings, each pairing a short passage from Stoic philosophers such as Marcus Aurelius, Seneca and Epictetus with a brief commentary. Monthly themes cover clarity, emotions, action and acceptance. Designed as a daily companion for reflection.

title: The Data Warehouse Toolkit
author: Ralph Kimball
description: Kimball and Ross explain dimensional modelling, the approach of organising data warehouse tables into facts and dimensions for analysis and reporting. Case studies from industries such as retail, insurance and finance demonstrate design patterns, slowly changing dimensions and best practices. Data engineers, analysts and architects building business intelligence systems use it as a practical design reference.

title: The Demon-Haunted World
author: Carl Sagan
description: Carl Sagan explains the scientific method and why critical thinking matters, using examples of pseudoscience, superstition and hoaxes. He offers a toolkit for evaluating claims. Valuable reading for students and anyone interested in reasoning and evidence.

title: The DevOps Handbook
author: Gene Kim
description: Kim and co-authors describe how organisations can deliver software faster and more reliably by improving the flow of work between development and operations. Chapters address continuous integration and deployment, telemetry, feedback loops and a culture of learning, with case studies from real companies. Engineering leaders, developers and operations staff will find a practical roadmap for adopting DevOps practices.

title: The Devil in the White City
author: Erik Larson
description: Larson interweaves two true stories from 1890s Chicago: architect Daniel Burnham's effort to build the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, and the crimes of H. H. Holmes, a killer who used the fair to find victims. Built from historical sources and written with the pacing of a novel, it suits readers who enjoy narrative history and true crime.

title: The Diary of a Young Girl
author: Anne Frank
description: Anne Frank's diary records the two years she and her family spent hiding from the Nazis in a concealed annex of an Amsterdam building. Writing between the ages of thirteen and fifteen, she describes life in close quarters, tensions among the residents, her hopes to become a writer and her growing self-awareness. It offers a personal, first-hand perspective on the Holocaust.

title: The Disappearing Spoon
author: Sam Kean
publisher: Little, Brown Books for Young Readers
description: Kean tells stories behind the elements of the periodic table, covering their discovery, uses and the people involved. The book links chemistry to history, war, medicine and everyday life. An entertaining companion to chemistry studies.

title: The Discovery of India
author: Jawaharlal Nehru
description: Written by Jawaharlal Nehru while imprisoned in 1942 to 1946, this book surveys Indian history, philosophy and culture from ancient times to the colonial period. It reflects his thinking about Indian identity and nationhood. An important text in Indian historical and political writing.

title: The Double Helix
author: James D. Watson
description: Watson gives his personal account of the race to determine the structure of DNA in the early 1950s, centred on his collaboration with Francis Crick in Cambridge. The memoir describes rivalries, mistakes and the role of other researchers, including Rosalind Franklin. Candid and often opinionated, it suits readers interested in how scientific discovery happens and the people behind it.

title: The E-Myth Revisited
author: Michael E. Gerber
description: Gerber argues that many small businesses fail because they are started by technicians who are good at their craft but not at running a company. He recommends working on the business rather than in it, by building documented systems in the manner of a franchise. Owners and would-be entrepreneurs will find a practical framework for creating a business that can run without them.

title: The Effective Executive
author: Peter F. Drucker
description: Drucker contends that effectiveness is a set of practices any knowledge worker can learn rather than an innate talent. He discusses managing time, focusing on contribution, building on strengths, setting priorities and making sound decisions. Concise and practical, it suits managers, professionals and anyone whose work requires them to direct their own efforts toward results.

title: The Elegant Universe
author: Brian Greene
description: Greene, a physicist, introduces string theory and the search for a single framework that reconciles general relativity with quantum mechanics. He builds up from Einstein's ideas about space and time and the strangeness of the quantum world before explaining vibrating strings and extra dimensions. Using analogies instead of equations, it suits general readers curious about modern theoretical physics.

title: The Elements of Computing Systems
author: Noam Nisan
description: Nisan and Schocken guide readers through building a complete computer system from first principles, starting with simple logic gates and progressing through hardware, an assembler, a virtual machine, a compiler and a basic operating system. Each chapter is a hands-on project using supplied simulation tools. Students and self-learners wanting to understand how computers work end to end will benefit.

title: The Elements of Statistical Learning
author: Trevor Hastie
description: A comprehensive textbook on statistical methods for machine learning, covering linear models, classification, kernel methods, model assessment, trees, boosting, neural networks, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Aimed at graduate students with mathematical background.

title: The Emperor of All Maladies
author: Siddhartha Mukherjee
description: Mukherjee, an oncologist, traces the history of cancer from ancient descriptions to modern genetics and targeted therapies. He follows the surgeons, researchers, activists and patients who shaped treatment, including the development of chemotherapy and debates over prevention. Combining science, history and clinical stories, it suits general readers who want to understand the disease and the long effort to fight it.

title: The Everything Store
author: Brad Stone
description: A journalist's account of the founding and growth of Amazon and the management style of Jeff Bezos. Based on interviews with current and former employees, it follows the company from an online bookstore to a global retailer and cloud provider. Of interest to business and technology readers.

title: The Fabric of the Cosmos
author: Brian Greene
description: Greene explores what physics reveals about the nature of space and time, examining questions such as why time seems to flow in one direction and whether space is a real entity. He covers relativity, quantum entanglement, cosmology and ideas from string theory. Written for non-specialists with analogies and minimal mathematics, it suits readers curious about the foundations of reality.

title: The Fire Next Time
author: James Baldwin
description: Two essays by James Baldwin on race, religion and American society, written as a letter to his nephew and a reflection on his own experiences. Published in 1963, it was influential during the civil rights movement. A short, powerful work for readers interested in history and social justice.

title: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
author: Patrick Lencioni
description: A fictional story of a new chief executive working to rebuild a struggling leadership team, followed by a practical model. Lencioni identifies five problems, from absence of trust to inattention to results, and how to address them. Widely used in team-building and management training.

title: The Founder's Dilemmas
author: Noam Wasserman
description: A Harvard professor uses data from thousands of start-ups to examine early decisions founders face, such as whether to found alone or with others, how to split equity and when to hire or raise money. He shows the trade-offs behind each choice. A research-based guide for founders.

title: The Four Agreements
author: Don Miguel Ruiz
description: Ruiz draws on Toltec spiritual ideas to offer four principles for personal freedom: being impeccable with your word, not taking things personally, not making assumptions and always doing your best. He explains how beliefs absorbed in childhood can create suffering and how these commitments can replace them. Short and accessible, it suits readers interested in practical spirituality and self-reflection.

title: The Four Steps to the Epiphany
author: Steven Gary Blank
description: Steve Blank introduces customer development, a process for discovering and validating customers alongside product development. The book outlines four stages from customer discovery to company building. A foundational text behind the lean start-up approach.

title: The Gene: An Intimate History
author: Siddhartha Mukherjee
description: Mukherjee recounts the history of genetics, from Mendel and Darwin through the discovery of DNA to gene editing and the sequencing of the human genome. He also discusses the misuse of genetic ideas in eugenics and the ethical questions raised by new technologies. Personal reflections on mental illness in his own family run through this accessible account for general readers.

title: The Gifts of Imperfection
author: Brené Brown
description: Brown, a researcher on shame and vulnerability, offers guidance on letting go of perfectionism and the need to please others. She outlines ten guideposts for what she calls wholehearted living, covering self-compassion, resilience, gratitude, creativity, rest and play. Readers seeking a gentle, research-informed approach to self-acceptance and emotional wellbeing will find practical reflections.

title: The Glass Castle
author: Jeannette Walls
description: Walls recounts growing up with a brilliant but alcoholic father and an artistic, unpredictable mother who moved the family between desert towns and a poor West Virginia mining community. The memoir describes poverty, neglect and the children's self-reliance without bitterness, and follows Walls's eventual move to New York. It suits readers interested in family memoirs and stories of resilience.

title: The Go Programming Language
author: Alan A. A. Donovan
description: Donovan and Kernighan present the Go language through practical, carefully chosen examples, covering basic syntax, composite types, functions, methods, interfaces and packages. Later chapters address goroutines and channels for concurrency, testing, reflection and low-level programming. Programmers with experience in another language who want a thorough, idiomatic introduction to Go will find it a solid tutorial and reference.

title: The Goal
author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt
description: Written as a novel, Goldratt's book follows Alex Rogo, a manager trying to rescue a failing manufacturing plant within a few months. Guided by a former teacher, he learns to identify bottlenecks and focus improvement on them, ideas that became known as the theory of constraints. It suits managers, engineers and students of operations who prefer learning through story.

title: The Goldfinch
author: Donna Tartt
description: After surviving an explosion at a New York museum that kills his mother, thirteen-year-old Theo Decker keeps a small Dutch painting taken from the wreckage. Tartt follows him into adulthood through New York, Las Vegas and Amsterdam as the painting draws him into the art underworld. This long, richly detailed novel suits readers who enjoy literary fiction about loss and obsession.

title: The Great Gatsby
author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
description: Narrated by Nick Carraway, the novel follows his mysterious neighbour Jay Gatsby, a wealthy man who throws lavish parties on Long Island in pursuit of Daisy Buchanan, the woman he once loved. Fitzgerald portrays the glamour and moral emptiness of the Jazz Age and the limits of the American Dream. It is a staple of classrooms and suits readers of classic literature.

title: The Guns of August
author: Barbara W. Tuchman
description: Tuchman narrates the opening month of the First World War, beginning with the diplomatic and military plans that preceded it and following the early campaigns on the Western Front and in East Prussia. She examines the decisions and miscalculations of leaders on all sides. Readers interested in military history and the origins of the war will find a vivid, detailed account.

title: The Hacker Playbook 3
author: Peter Kim
description: Kim presents penetration testing from a red team perspective, walking through realistic attack scenarios against corporate networks. Topics include reconnaissance, web exploitation, compromising networks, moving laterally, escalating privileges and evading detection. Intended for security professionals and students with some technical background, it emphasises hands-on labs and should be used only for authorised testing and learning.

title: The Handmaid's Tale
author: Margaret Atwood
description: In the Republic of Gilead, a theocratic regime that has replaced part of the United States, Offred is a Handmaid assigned to bear children for a powerful Commander and his wife. Atwood's novel tells her story through memories of her former life and the restricted present. It explores power, control over women's bodies and resistance, and suits readers of dystopian and literary fiction.

title: The Happiness Advantage
author: Shawn Achor
description: Achor draws on positive psychology research to argue that happiness tends to fuel success at work, rather than simply following it. He outlines seven principles, such as training the brain to notice opportunities, making small manageable changes and investing in social support. Professionals, managers and readers interested in workplace wellbeing will find practical, research-based suggestions.

title: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
author: Ben Horowitz
description: Horowitz, a venture capitalist and former chief executive, writes about the hardest parts of building and running a company, drawing on his experience leading a struggling technology business. He discusses layoffs, firing executives, managing through crises, building culture and the psychological strain on leaders. Founders and managers facing difficult decisions will find candid advice grounded in real situations.

title: The Hidden Life of Trees
author: Peter Wohlleben
description: Wohlleben, a German forester, describes how trees in a forest interact, drawing on scientific research and his own observations. He explains how trees may share nutrients through root and fungal networks, respond to threats and support their offspring. Written in an approachable, sometimes personal style, it suits nature lovers and general readers curious about forest ecology.

title: The Histories
author: Herodotus
description: Written in the fifth century BC, Herodotus's account of the wars between the Greeks and the Persian Empire is often called the first work of history. Alongside the conflict, it describes the customs, geography and stories of many ancient peoples. Essential reading for students of the ancient world.

title: The History of the Ancient World
author: Susan Wise Bauer
description: Bauer surveys the ancient world from the earliest written records through the fall of Rome, moving between Mesopotamia, Egypt, India, China, Greece and other regions. She focuses on rulers, wars and the stories societies told about themselves, presented in short chronological chapters. It suits general readers and homeschool families wanting a readable narrative overview of ancient history.

title: The Hobbit
author: J.R.R. Tolkien
description: Bilbo Baggins, a comfort-loving hobbit, is recruited by the wizard Gandalf to join thirteen dwarves on a quest to reclaim their treasure from the dragon Smaug. The journey takes him through encounters with trolls, goblins, elves and giant spiders, and he gains courage along the way. Tolkien's fantasy adventure suits younger readers and adults alike.

title: The Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book
author: Andriy Burkov
description: Burkov condenses the core ideas of machine learning into a short book, covering supervised and unsupervised learning, key algorithms, neural networks, model evaluation and practical issues such as feature engineering. Explanations use mathematical notation but stay brief. It suits practitioners wanting a quick refresher and students seeking a compact map of the field before moving to deeper texts.

title: The Hunger Games
author: Suzanne Collins
description: In the nation of Panem, a ruling Capitol forces each district to send two young people to fight to the death in a televised contest. Sixteen-year-old Katniss Everdeen volunteers to take her younger sister's place. Collins's dystopian novel explores survival, inequality and media spectacle, and suits teens and adults who enjoy fast-paced speculative fiction.

title: The Illustrated Network
author: Walter Goralski
description: A textbook that explains TCP/IP networking using real packet captures and configurations from a working network. It covers protocols from the link layer to applications, along with routing and security. Useful for students who learn by example.

title: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks
author: Rebecca Skloot
description: Skloot tells the story of Henrietta Lacks, a Black woman whose cancer cells were taken without her knowledge in 1951 and became the first human cell line to grow indefinitely in a laboratory. She traces the cells' role in medical research alongside the experiences of the Lacks family. The book raises questions about consent, race and ethics in science.

title: The Index Card
author: Helaine Olen
description: Olen and Pollack argue that sound personal finance advice is simple enough to fit on an index card. They expand on a short list of rules, such as saving a meaningful share of income, paying off credit cards, using low-cost index funds and being wary of financial salespeople. The book suits readers wanting straightforward guidance without complex strategies.

title: The Inevitable
author: Kevin Kelly
description: Kevin Kelly identifies twelve long-term technological trends, such as sharing, tracking, remixing and filtering, that he expects to shape the coming decades. Each chapter explains a trend and its likely effects on everyday life. A forward-looking read on digital culture.

title: The Innovator's Dilemma
author: Clayton M. Christensen
description: Christensen examines why well-managed, successful companies often lose their leading positions when new technologies emerge. He distinguishes sustaining innovations from disruptive ones that start in small or low-end markets and later overtake incumbents, using industries such as disk drives as case studies. Managers, strategists and business students will find an influential framework for thinking about technological change.

title: The Innovators
author: Walter Isaacson
description: Isaacson traces the history of the digital revolution, from Ada Lovelace's ideas about computing machines through the invention of the computer, transistor, microchip, personal computer, internet and web. He emphasises that innovation usually came from collaboration among teams rather than lone geniuses. Readers interested in technology history and the people behind it will find an engaging group portrait.

title: The Intelligent Investor
author: Benjamin Graham
description: Graham sets out the philosophy of value investing, stressing the difference between investing and speculation, the importance of a margin of safety and the need to control emotions during market swings. He contrasts defensive and enterprising investors and explains how to analyse securities. Later editions add commentary relating his ideas to modern markets, making it useful for long-term investors.

title: The Kite Runner
author: Khaled Hosseini
description: Amir, a boy from a wealthy family in Kabul, betrays his loyal friend Hassan, a servant's son, and carries the guilt into adulthood after fleeing to the United States. Years later he returns to a Taliban-ruled Afghanistan seeking redemption. Hosseini's novel explores friendship, fathers and sons, and a country's upheavals, and suits readers of contemporary literary fiction.

title: The Last Lecture
author: Randy Pausch
description: Computer science professor Randy Pausch expands on his final lecture, given after learning he had terminal cancer. He reflects on childhood dreams, enabling the dreams of others and living well. A moving and widely read book.

title: The Lean Mindset
author: Mary Poppendieck
description: Mary and Tom Poppendieck apply lean thinking to software and product development, emphasising purpose, customer focus, energised teams and learning through experimentation. Drawing on examples from various organisations, they discuss how teams can deliver value quickly while staying aligned with real needs. Product managers, engineering leaders and agile practitioners will find ideas for building effective, motivated teams.

title: The Lean Product Playbook
author: Dan Olsen
description: Olsen offers a step-by-step process for building products customers want, organised around achieving product-market fit. Stages include identifying target customers and their unmet needs, defining a value proposition, specifying a minimum viable product, prototyping and testing with users. Product managers, founders and designers will find concrete frameworks and examples for reducing risk when developing new products.

title: The Lean Startup
author: Eric Ries
description: Ries proposes a scientific approach to building new ventures under conditions of uncertainty. Central ideas include the build-measure-learn loop, minimum viable products, validated learning, actionable metrics and deciding when to pivot or persevere. Founders, product teams and managers launching new initiatives inside larger organisations will find a practical method for testing ideas before investing heavily.

title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up
author: Marie Kondo
description: Marie Kondo describes her method of decluttering by category and keeping only items that genuinely matter to the owner. The book covers how to sort clothes, books, papers and keepsakes, and how to store what remains. Helpful for readers who want an orderly living or study space.

title: The Little Book That Still Beats the Market
author: Joel Greenblatt
description: A hedge fund manager explains a simple, rules-based approach to value investing, often called the magic formula, that ranks companies by earnings yield and return on capital. He uses everyday examples to show why buying good businesses at bargain prices works over time. Written for beginners to stock investing.

title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing
author: John C. Bogle
description: Bogle, founder of Vanguard, makes the case for buying and holding a low-cost fund that tracks the whole stock market. He explains how fees, trading costs and taxes erode returns for active investors, and why most fund managers fail to beat the market over time. Concise and data-driven, it suits new and experienced investors seeking a simple long-term strategy.

title: The Lord of the Rings
author: J.R.R. Tolkien
description: Frodo Baggins inherits a powerful ring created by the Dark Lord Sauron and sets out with a fellowship of companions to destroy it before it can be reclaimed. Tolkien's epic follows their journey across Middle-earth through war, friendship and sacrifice. With its invented languages, histories and detailed world-building, it suits readers who enjoy immersive high fantasy.

title: The Lost City of Z
author: David Grann
description: Grann retraces the expedition of British explorer Percy Fawcett, who disappeared in the Amazon in 1925 while searching for a lost civilisation. The book alternates between Fawcett's story and the author's own journey into the rainforest. Adventure history mixed with modern archaeology.

title: The Lucifer Effect
author: Philip Zimbardo
description: Zimbardo examines how ordinary people come to commit cruel acts, drawing heavily on his 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment, which he recounts in detail. He links its lessons to the abuses at Abu Ghraib prison and argues that situations and systems shape behaviour more than is often assumed. The final chapters turn to resisting harmful social pressure and to everyday heroism, making it useful for students of social psychology and ethics.

title: The Magic of Thinking Big
author: David J. Schwartz
